tales.title: Why we live on Prairie Avenue
text: When the great fire came in October of 1871, it started on the West Side and the wind drove it north and east, across the river, through the whole business district and the North Side, where most of the fine houses were. It never came this far south. Prairie Avenue was spared.

So afterwards, everybody who could afford it came here. Within ten years this was the finest street in Chicago, stone and brick houses side by side for six blocks, and every man in them had made a fortune or was making one. The old families still say they live on the Avenue as if there were no other. There are others now. But for thirty years, there were not.

tales.title: Everyone is moving north
text: Since Mr. Potter Palmer built his castle on the Lake Shore Drive, the fashionable people have been going north, one after another. The young couples do not want a house on Prairie Avenue. They want one on the Drive, or in Lake Forest, away from the railroad.

The Illinois Central runs along the lake behind us, and the trains go by day and night, and the smoke comes over the gardens. And to the west and south of us, the town is creeping up: boarding houses, saloons, the Levee district on Twenty-second Street, which no lady will mention by name. My father built this house to last a hundred years. I do not think his grandchildren will live in it.

tales.title: The White City
text: Eleven years ago, in the summer of 1893, Chicago held the World's Columbian Exposition in Jackson Park, and the whole world came to see it. Great white palaces around a lagoon, lit at night by electricity, more light than anybody had ever seen in one place. And Mr. Ferris's wheel, taller than any building in the city, turning slowly with a whole street car full of people in every car.

I went forty times. Everybody did. People came from every country in the world and stood in the Court of Honour at night with their mouths open. They called it the White City. Then it ended, and that winter the palaces stood empty, and the next summer most of them burned. It was like a dream that everybody had at once.

tales.title: The last night of the fair
text: On the last week of the fair, Mayor Carter Harrison gave a speech to the visiting mayors of America, and said Chicago had shown the world what it could do. That evening a young man came to his front door on Ashland Avenue, asked to see him, and shot him three times.

The fair's closing ceremonies were cancelled. Instead of fireworks, there was a funeral. I had shaken the mayor's hand a week before. He was a big, loud, generous man who wore a slouch hat and rode about the city on horseback and knew every saloon keeper in the city by name, and half the respectable people hated him, and they all went to his funeral.

tales.title: The bomb in the Haymarket
text: In May of 1886 the workingmen of Chicago struck for an eight hour day. There was a meeting in the Haymarket on Randolph Street, anarchists speaking from a wagon. When the police marched in to break it up, someone threw a bomb into their ranks. Seven policemen died of it, and more people in the shooting afterwards.

Nobody ever proved who threw the bomb. They tried eight anarchists for it and hanged four. Some men on this street said it was justice. Some said it was not. I have never been sure. When the governor pardoned the three who were left, eleven years ago, half the city called him a traitor. The other half called him brave.

tales.title: The summer of the strike
text: Ten summers ago the workers at Mr. Pullman's car works went on strike, after he cut their wages and would not lower their rents in his town. The railway union refused to handle Pullman cars, and every railroad in the West stopped. No trains went in or out of Chicago.

President Cleveland sent the army. There were soldiers camped on the lake front and fires in the railroad yards and mobs in the streets, and the men on Prairie Avenue sat up at night with pistols in their desks. In the end the strike was broken and the union man Debs went to jail. Mr. Pullman was never the same afterwards, and neither were the people of his town.

tales.title: The wheat corner
text: Seven years ago a young man named Joe Leiter, son of old Levi Leiter, tried to corner the wheat market at the Board of Trade. He bought every bushel of wheat he could find, and for months he drove the price up and up, and everybody said he was a genius.

But old Phil Armour was selling against him, and Armour sent ships into the ice of Lake Superior with tugs to break a channel and bring down the wheat from the Northwest in the dead of winter. When spring came there was wheat everywhere, and the price collapsed, and young Leiter lost millions. His father paid. I watched it all from the gallery. That is the Board of Trade. Fortunes in an afternoon, and gone by the next.

tales.title: Buildings that touch the sky
text: When I was a young man, a building of five storeys was tall. Now there are buildings downtown of sixteen, twenty, twenty-two storeys, built on frames of steel, with the walls hung on them like curtains, and elevators to carry you to the top in a minute.

The Masonic Temple has a roof garden twenty storeys up, where you can look out over the whole city and the lake. The architects of this city have invented a new kind of building, and New York has copied it. My office is on the fourteenth floor. In the morning, when the smoke is low, I look down on it like a man in a balloon. I can see the ships coming in thirty miles off.

tales.title: Going downtown
text: Every morning at half past eight my carriage takes me downtown to my office on LaSalle Street, a mile and a half, and every evening at half past five it brings me home. Some of my neighbours take the cable car, which runs up State Street, or the elevated railway, which runs down the alley west of State Street.

My father walked to work, along the lake shore, with his dinner in a pail. I could walk if I liked. I do not like. The streets downtown are so crowded with wagons and cars and carriages that it can take half an hour to cross State Street. A gentleman's time is worth more than that. So is his collar.

tales.title: When I was a soldier
text: I was nineteen when the war began, and I went with an Illinois regiment, and I was at Shiloh and at Vicksburg. I have not talked about it much since. Most of the men on this street my age did not go. They hired substitutes, or they were too busy making money. That was allowed.

On Decoration Day I go out to the cemetery with the old soldiers of my post and we lay flowers on the graves. There are fewer of us every year. Last month there were eleven. When the young men talk about war, about Cuba and the Philippines, I listen and say nothing. They had a short war. Ours was four years.

tales.title: The war with Spain
text: Six years ago, when the Maine was blown up in Havana harbour, every young man in Chicago wanted to go and fight Spain. The First Illinois went to Cuba and were at the siege of Santiago, and more of them died of the fever than of the Spanish bullets.

My son went. He came home thin and yellow with the malaria, and he has never been quite strong since. He says it was worth it. They freed Cuba, he says, and they took the Philippines, and the flag goes around the world now. Then he coughs. I am proud of him. I wish he had stayed at home.

tales.title: Turning the river backwards
text: Four years ago, Chicago did something no city had ever done. It made its river run backwards. For years the river had carried all the sewage of the city out into the lake, where the city drinks. When the rains were heavy, the typhoid and the cholera came.

So they dug a great canal from the South Branch to the Des Plaines River, twenty-eight miles through rock, deeper and wider than any canal in the world. In January of 1900 they opened the gates, and the river turned around and began to flow away from the lake, toward the Mississippi and St. Louis. St. Louis sued. Chicago does not care. Chicago never cares what anybody thinks.

tales.title: The convention last week
text: Last week the Republican party held its national convention at the Coliseum on Wabash Avenue and nominated President Roosevelt for another term. The city was full of delegates and bands and banners. Every hotel was booked, every saloon was full, and you could not get a cab for love or money.

I went to two sessions. It was very hot and very loud and nothing was in doubt, since everybody knew it would be Roosevelt. But it was a fine show. They say the Democrats meet in St. Louis next week, where the World's Fair is open. If the Republicans can win Illinois with Roosevelt, they can win the country. I think they can. Most of this street thinks so too.

tales.title: The new university
text: Twelve years ago a new university opened on the Midway, beside where the fair would be, built on Mr. Rockefeller's millions. Now it has grey stone towers like Oxford, and professors from all over the world, and students, men and women both, studying side by side. President Harper says it will be the greatest university in America.

The old families send their sons east to Yale and Harvard, as they always have. But the new university is changing Chicago. It has brought scholars to a city that only had merchants. A man on this street used to be ashamed to read a book in public. Now there is a professor at every dinner party, and the ladies hang on every word.

tales.title: What a fortune is for
text: The men on this street have given Chicago a great deal. A museum, an art institute, a library, a university, hospitals, an orchestra. Some of them did it because they believed in it, and some of them did it so that people would forget how they made their money.

My father used to say: a man who dies rich dies disgraced. That was Mr. Carnegie's saying, and my father repeated it often. He did not die poor, mind you. But he gave the money for a hospital ward and a school, and the nurses in that ward still put flowers by his portrait on his birthday. That is a better monument than this house.

tales.title: The trust
text: Two years ago the five biggest makers of reaping machines in the country joined together into one great company, the International Harvester. Mr. Morgan's bankers arranged it. The newspapers call it a trust and say it will crush the farmer.

I say the farmer has never had better machines at lower prices. But the President is in a fighting mood against the trusts, and his attorney general is going after the railroad combinations in the courts. Everything is getting bigger. Companies are getting bigger, cities are getting bigger, fortunes are getting bigger. I sometimes wonder where it stops.

tales.title: Calling day
text: Every lady on this street has an at home day, when she receives callers in the afternoon. Mine is Tuesday. From three until six, ladies come in their carriages, leave their cards on the silver tray in the hall, come in for a quarter of an hour, take a cup of tea, talk about nothing, and leave. Then they go and call on somebody else.

It sounds very silly, and it is. But it is also how everything on this street is done. A marriage, a charity, a quarrel, a reconciliation: all begin with a card on a tray. If a lady leaves a card with the corner turned down, she came herself. If she does not come back, something is wrong. You can read the whole history of Prairie Avenue in the cards on my hall table.

tales.title: Dressing for the day
text: A lady on this street changes her clothes four or five times a day. A morning dress for breakfast and the household. A walking dress to go out. A visiting dress for calls. A tea gown for the afternoon at home. A dinner dress at night, cut low, with jewels. Each with its own hat and gloves and shoes.

My maid spends half her day dressing me and undressing me and putting my things away. I spend a great deal of money at Field's and at the dressmaker's. My husband says I could clothe an army on what I spend in a year. I tell him an army does not dine with the Fields.

tales.title: Miss Addams on Halsted Street
text: Fifteen years ago Miss Jane Addams took an old house on Halsted Street, in the middle of the poorest ward on the West Side, and went to live there among the immigrants: Italians, Greeks, Russian Jews, Bohemians. She calls it Hull House. She runs a kindergarten, a night school, a bath house, a theatre, a public kitchen, and a club for working girls.

Some of the ladies of this street give her money. A few of us go and teach. I have a class of Italian girls on Thursday nights, sewing and English. They work ten hours a day in the garment shops, and then they come and sit in my class and learn, and laugh. My husband thinks I go to a church sewing circle. In a way, I do.

tales.title: My friend at the Iroquois
text: My friend took her two little girls to the Iroquois Theatre on the thirtieth of December, for the holiday matinee, with their nurse. They had seats in the balcony. When the fire started on the stage, the people in the balcony rushed for the doors, and the doors were locked, or opened inward, and the crowd pressed against them.

They found my friend afterwards in the stairway, with her arms around both her girls. The nurse lived. She was below them on the stairs and was pulled out by a fireman. She comes to see me sometimes, and we sit together and do not say much. The theatre had been open five weeks. They advertised it as absolutely fireproof.

tales.title: The servant problem
text: Every lady on this street complains about servants. A good cook is impossible to find. A good parlour maid stays a year and then marries the grocer's boy. The Irish girls are clever but quick tempered. The Swedish girls are steady but they leave to go to the factories, where they have their evenings free.

I have had the same cook for eleven years. I pay her more than any cook on the Avenue, and I give her two afternoons a week instead of one, and I have never once gone into her kitchen without knocking. The other ladies think I spoil her. My dinners are the best on the street. I have no servant problem at all.

tales.title: The vote
text: There are women in Chicago now who want the vote. They hold meetings, they march, they write to the newspapers. My husband says it is ridiculous. A woman's place is in the home, he says, and her influence is through her husband and her sons.

Women can vote in Colorado, and Wyoming, and Utah, and Idaho, and nothing terrible has happened there. Here in Illinois we can vote for school officers and the trustees of the state university, and nothing else. I do not march. But I have started to read the newspapers that my husband leaves on the breakfast table, all of them, the political pages too. When the time comes, I want to know what I am voting for.

tales.title: Mr. Thomas's orchestra
text: Thirteen years ago some of the men of Chicago persuaded Mr. Theodore Thomas to come from New York and build an orchestra here. He has given us Beethoven and Brahms and Wagner every week in the season, and he has fought with everybody, and he has never once given the public a cheap programme to please them.

The orchestra has always played in the Auditorium, which is too big for it. So this year the city raised the money to build him a hall of his own, on Michigan Avenue, and they are building it now. Mrs. Glessner has been one of his truest friends. Go and see her. She will tell you about the evenings Mr. Thomas spent at her table, talking music until midnight.

tales.title: The bicycle
text: Ten years ago, every lady in Chicago learned to ride a bicycle. It was a madness. We wore divided skirts and shirtwaists and straw hats, and rode out along the boulevards in parties, twenty or thirty of us, ringing our bells. Some of the gentlemen were scandalised. Some of the clergy preached against it.

I learned at forty-two, on the gravel paths in Washington Park, with my coachman running alongside to catch me. I fell off eleven times. The twelfth time I did not fall, and I rode all the way to the lake and back. I had never been anywhere by myself before, without a carriage or a maid or a husband. It was the most free I have ever felt.

tales.title: In mourning
text: When my husband died, I wore black crêpe for a year, and black silk for a year after that, and grey and lavender for six months more. For the first year I did not go out in society at all, and I received only family. My writing paper had a black border an inch wide.

It is the custom, and I followed it. But I will tell you something. In that first year, alone in this house, I read every book in my husband's library, which he never let me touch. I learned to keep the household accounts and I found out that our man of business had been cheating us for ten years. I dismissed him. Nobody on this street knows that. They think I sat in the dark and wept.

tales.title: Going away for the summer
text: In two weeks we close the house and go away for the summer: to the house on the lake in Wisconsin, or to the White Mountains, or to the sea at Bar Harbor. Everybody on the Avenue goes. By the end of July, the street is empty, the blinds are drawn, and the furniture is under dust sheets.

We take most of the servants and forty trunks and the horses go by special car. It is like an army moving. Then we come back in September, browner and fatter, and the season begins again. Chicago in August is impossible: hot, stinking, full of flies. I do not know how the people who have to stay here bear it. I suppose they do not have a choice.

tales.title: My garden
text: I have a little garden behind this house, between the back porch and the stable, and it is mine. I planted the roses myself, and the lilies, and the peonies that come up every June, as big as cabbages. My gardener does the digging. I do the rest.

The soot is terrible for roses, and the lake wind is worse. I wash the leaves by hand. My friends think I am eccentric. In the evenings, when the trains have gone by and the dust settles, I sit out there with a book and the smell of the roses, and for a quarter of an hour I could be anywhere. That is enough. That is what a garden is for.

tales.title: Talking to my sister in New York
text: Last month, for the first time, I talked to my sister in New York by long distance telephone. The operator called me back at three o'clock, and there was her voice, very small and crackling, from a thousand miles away. We had not heard each other's voice in four years.

We talked for three minutes, which cost my husband a fortune. Neither of us could think of anything to say. We just said: is that really you? And: how are the children? And: it is very hot here. Then the operator said time, and it was over. I sat down and cried. My husband thought something had happened. Something had.

tales.title: Home from college
text: I have just come home from my third year at Yale, and I am bored to death. In New Haven there was football and rowing and the clubs and the night before the game against Harvard when the whole town went mad. Here there is my mother's at home day and dinners with old men who talk about wheat.

My father wants me to come into the firm when I graduate. He started as a clerk at sixteen and built the business with his own hands, and he does not understand why I want to do anything else. I want to be an architect. I want to build things, like Mr. Burnham and Mr. Sullivan. My father says architects do not get rich. I say neither do clerks, mostly.

tales.title: My automobile
text: I bought an automobile in the spring, a little Winton with a two cylinder engine and a brass horn. It goes twenty miles an hour on a good road. The roads around Chicago are mostly not good. I have been stuck in the mud on the way to Lake Forest four times and been pulled out by a farmer's horse each time. The farmers laugh at me.

My father refuses to ride in it. My mother rode once, in a veil and goggles, and said never again. The coachman hates it, because it frightens his horses. But I tell you, in twenty years there will not be a horse left on this street. Everybody will have one of these. Everybody will laugh about the time they laughed at me.

tales.title: The big game
text: Last Thanksgiving I went to see the University of Chicago play Michigan at Marshall Field. Not the man, the field, named for him because he gave the land. Thousands of people in the stands, with flags and horns, in the cold. Michigan had not lost a game in three years.

Mr. Stagg's boys fought them for every yard. It was the hardest football I have ever seen, with men carried off the field one after another. In the end Michigan beat us badly, and Chicago's men walked off the field crying like babies. I lost my voice for a week. My mother says football should be outlawed. Half the country agrees with her.

tales.title: A summer at the settlement
text: This summer I am living at the university's settlement near the stockyards, back of the yards, as they call it. Miss McDowell runs it. I teach English to Polish and Lithuanian boys in the evening, and I see how the people live who work in the packing houses.

Six families in a frame house built for one. No water but a pump in the yard. The smell of the yards over everything. Men who work ten hours on the killing floor and come home with their hands cut to pieces. My father's money comes from shares in a packing company. I have not told him where I am spending my summer. I do not know what I am going to say when he asks.

tales.title: My first job
text: I started work in my father's bank on the first of June, as a junior clerk, at twelve dollars a week. My father said I must learn the business from the bottom, as he did. So I sit at a high desk in a back room on LaSalle Street and copy figures into ledgers for nine hours a day.

The other clerks know who my father is. They are very polite to me and they do not invite me to lunch. I eat a sandwich at my desk and look out of the window at the street. Someday I will have my father's office, with the big window and the leather chair. Today I have a stool and a pen that leaks.

tales.title: Going to the fair at St. Louis
text: Next week my brother and I are going down to St. Louis on the train to see the World's Fair, the Louisiana Purchase Exposition. They say it is bigger than our fair in 1893. They say there are palaces of electricity and machinery and agriculture, and a great wheel, and villages of people from all over the world, the Philippines and Africa and Japan, and Mr. Ferris's own wheel, carried down from Chicago and set up again.

My father says nothing will ever be as fine as the White City. He says St. Louis is only copying Chicago. Maybe. But I was only a boy in 1893, and I remember the lights and the wheel and nothing else. This time I am going to see everything. I have a list. It is four pages long.

tales.title: The boys who robbed the car barn
text: Last August four young men robbed the car barn of the Chicago City Railway, out at Sixty-first Street, and shot two clerks dead for two thousand dollars of the payroll. They called them the car barn bandits. They were about my age. They had been to school, some of them. One of them had a mother who took in sewing.

The police chased them all over the country until the winter, and at last they found them in a dugout in the Indiana dunes. They shot a detective dead there before they were taken. Three of them were hanged this spring. I followed the trial in every newspaper. I keep asking myself what turned them. Nobody can tell me.

tales.title: My coming out
text: Last winter I came out, which means I was presented to society at a ball my mother gave for me at the Auditorium, with four hundred guests and an orchestra and banks of white roses. I wore white satin from Paris, and I danced every dance, and I did not sleep for two days.

Since then I have been to forty dances, and twenty dinners, and a hundred teas. I have been proposed to twice, by a boy I danced with once and by a man of forty with a moustache. I said no to both. My mother says I must say yes to somebody by the end of next season. I would like to say yes to somebody I can talk to. That seems to be very difficult to arrange.

tales.title: I want to go to college
text: My brother is at Harvard. My cousin is at Yale. I wanted to go to Vassar, or Smith, or to the new university here, where women study alongside the men. My father said no. A girl does not need college, he said. A girl needs a husband and a household.

So I am taking lessons at home. French, music, drawing, a little history from a tutor who comes on Tuesdays. I read every book my brother leaves in the house when he comes home for the summer, and when he goes back to Harvard, I know more than he does. He knows it, too. He does not say so to our father.

tales.title: Lessons at the Art Institute
text: I take classes at the Art Institute three mornings a week, in the school behind the galleries. We draw from plaster casts, and from life. Not from the nude, of course, not the ladies' class. From a man in a suit, or a woman in a dress, sitting very still.

My teacher says I have a real talent. He says I could exhibit, if I worked hard. My mother says a lady may paint as a pastime but not as a profession. So I paint as a pastime, five hours a day, and I have a portfolio under my bed of two hundred drawings. Some day I am going to show them to someone who will say yes.

tales.title: The hat
text: I bought a hat yesterday at Field's. It is the largest hat on Prairie Avenue. It has a brim a foot and a half across, a whole stuffed bird on it with its wings spread, ostrich plumes, a bow of violet velvet, and a veil. It cost forty dollars. My mother nearly fainted.

I wore it to church this morning and three ladies behind me could not see the minister. One of them said something to me afterwards that I shall not repeat. I do not care. It is a magnificent hat. The bird is a tern. I named him Henry.

tales.title: Tennis on the lawn
text: On summer afternoons we play lawn tennis on the court behind the Keiths' house, or at the club. The girls play in long white skirts and shirtwaists with sleeves to the wrist, and straw hats tied on with veils. It is very hot. We play anyway.

I am the best player on the Avenue, man or woman. The young men do not like it. They play hard against me for a set and then say they have a headache. I beat my brother six games to love last week, and he has not spoken to me since. My mother says a young lady should let the gentleman win. I say then she should find me a gentleman who can.

tales.title: My engagement
text: I am engaged. He is a lawyer, twenty-eight years old, from Boston, with a moustache and a good income and very kind eyes. We met at a dinner last autumn and he wrote to me every week all winter. In May he asked my father, and my father said yes, and then he asked me, and I said yes.

We are to be married in October, at Second Presbyterian, and we will live on the North Side near the lake. My mother is planning the wedding like a military campaign. I would be happy with a small wedding in the parlour. Nobody asks what I would like. That is all right. In October, I will be the one who gets to decide.

tales.title: My diary
text: I have kept a diary since I was ten years old. Every night before bed I write in it: what I did, who I saw, what they said, what I thought about it. I have nine volumes now, bound in red leather, in a locked drawer in my desk.

My diary knows more about this street than anybody. Who is in love with whom. Who is quarrelling. Which family has had losses at the Board of Trade and is selling the horses. In a hundred years, somebody may read it and know what it was like to be a girl on Prairie Avenue. They will think we were very silly. Some of us were. Not all.

tales.title: My pony
text: I have a pony named Biscuit, who lives in our stable with the carriage horses. He is fat and brown and very naughty, and he bites the coachman when nobody is looking. The coachman says he is the devil in a pony's skin.

On fine mornings the groom puts the little saddle on him and leads me up and down the alley, and then out on the street, very slow, past all the houses. All the other children wave. One day the groom let go of the rope and Biscuit ran all the way to the corner with me holding on to his mane, and I did not fall off, and the groom turned white. I was not scared at all. Not much.

tales.title: The Fourth of July
text: In three days it will be the Fourth of July, and we are going to have firecrackers. My father bought a whole box of them, and Roman candles, and pinwheels, and sparklers, and at night we will set them off in the yard behind the house, and everybody on the street will do the same.

Last year a boy on the next street blew off the end of his thumb with a cannon cracker. My mother says I may only have the little crackers and the sparklers. I am saving my pocket money for a cannon cracker anyway. I will set it off very carefully, behind the stable, where my mother will not see. Do not tell anybody.

tales.title: The schoolroom on the top floor
text: I do not go to school. School comes to me. There is a schoolroom on the top floor of our house, with a blackboard and a globe and a map of the world, and a governess who comes every morning at nine and stays until one.

I learn reading and writing and sums and geography and French and the piano. I am very good at geography and very bad at the piano. My governess says I have no ear. I can name every river in Europe and every capital in South America. When I am grown up I am going to go and see all of them. The piano I am going to leave at home.

tales.title: Dancing school
text: On Saturday mornings I go to dancing school with all the other children of the street, in a hall downtown, with a master in a tail coat who plays the violin and counts out loud. One, two, three. One, two, three. Point your toe.

The boys have to wear white gloves and bow to the girls and ask them to dance. The girls have to curtsy and say yes. You cannot say no, even to the boy who steps on your feet. There is a boy who always steps on mine. He says he does it on purpose because he likes me. I said that was a very stupid way to show it.

tales.title: Down at the lake
text: Behind our house, across the railroad tracks, is the lake. We are not supposed to go there because of the trains. But the nurse takes us over the bridge across the tracks sometimes, and we go down to the shore and throw stones and watch the ships.

The lake is so big you cannot see the other side. It looks like the ocean. In a storm the waves come right over the breakwater and spray all the way to the tracks. My big brother says there are ships at the bottom of the lake, hundreds of them, with drowned sailors still inside. I do not believe him. I look anyway, every time.

tales.title: The circus came to town
text: In May the circus came to Chicago, with three rings at once and a parade down Michigan Avenue with elephants and camels and a lion in a cage on wheels, and a steam calliope playing tunes that you could hear for a mile.

We went on a Saturday afternoon, all the children and both nurses. I saw a lady standing on the back of a galloping horse, and a man put his head in a lion's mouth, and twelve clowns came out of one little carriage. When I am grown I am going to join the circus. I am going to be the man with the lion. My nurse says the lion will eat me. I say not if I am very polite.

tales.title: The bear at Lincoln Park
text: Last Sunday we drove all the way up to Lincoln Park, on the North Side, to see the animals. There are buffaloes and deer and eagles and monkeys, and a big brown bear in a pit who stands up on his back legs and begs for peanuts.

I threw him a peanut and he caught it in his mouth. Then I threw him another one and it hit him on the nose and he looked at me very sadly. I felt so bad I gave him all my peanuts. My father said the bear was the cleverest beggar in Chicago. He said there were men on LaSalle Street who could learn from him.

tales.title: The electric light
text: In our house, when you turn the little brass key on the wall, the lights come on. Electric light, my father says, from wires that come all the way from a power house downtown. My grandmother still does not trust it. She keeps a candle and a box of matches on her nightstand, just in case.

Once there was a thunderstorm and all the lights went out, all over the street, and everybody had to light the old gas lamps. My grandmother sat in her room with her candle and said: I told you so. I told you so. I think she was pleased.

tales.title: The new baby
text: There is a new baby in our house. She came in the night, and in the morning my nurse took me in to see her. She is very small and very red and she does not do anything but sleep and cry. Everybody says she is beautiful. I do not think she is beautiful at all.

But yesterday she held my finger very tight, with her whole hand, and looked at me. My nurse says babies cannot see very well yet. I think she saw me. I am going to teach her to ride my pony when she is bigger. And to climb trees. And not to cry so much.

tales.title: The ice cream
text: On Sunday, after church, the cook makes ice cream in the freezer in the yard, with ice and salt and a handle you have to turn. My brother and I take turns turning it. It takes a whole hour and your arm feels like it will fall off.

Then the cook opens it and there it is, vanilla, with real cream, so cold it hurts your teeth. And the cook gives us the dasher to lick, the paddle from inside, which has the most ice cream on it of anything. That is the best part of the whole week. Better than church. Do not tell the minister.

tales.title: My ball
text: I have a ball. It is red. It goes bounce. It went under the big chair and Nanny got it out.
I threw it at the dog. The dog ran away. Then the dog came back and I threw it again. Nanny says that is enough. It is not enough.

tales.title: The big horses
text: The big horses live in the stable. They say huff, huff. They have big feet.
The man in the hat lifted me up to touch the brown one. It was warm. Its nose was soft, like my blanket. It blew on my face. I laughed. I want to see the horses again.

tales.title: The big water
text: We went to the big water. It goes swish, swish. It is cold. It got my shoes wet.
Nanny said no, no. I found a stone. It is white and smooth. It is in my pocket. You can hold it. Give it back.

tales.title: Choo choo
text: The train goes choo choo, past the garden. It is very loud. It makes the windows shake.
I wave at the train. The man on the train waved back. He did. He waved at me. Tomorrow I will wave again.

tales.title: Thursday afternoon
text: Every maid on Prairie Avenue lives for Thursday afternoon. That is our afternoon off, from two o'clock until ten, and every Sunday after the breakfast dishes, every second week. On Thursday the streetcars going north are full of girls in their best hats, going to see their sisters and their sweethearts and the shops on State Street.

I go to my cousin's in the Swedish quarter on the North Side, and we drink coffee and eat cardamom bread and speak our own language for six hours, and nobody rings a bell for me. At half past nine I am on the car again, and at ten I am in my attic room with my uniform laid out for six o'clock. Six hours of being myself. It is enough to last the week. Nearly.

tales.title: The bells
text: In the back hall of this house there is a board with forty little bells on springs, one for every room, each with a name painted underneath: Library, Parlour, Mrs. G's Room, Front Door, Guest Room North. When someone in the family presses a button in a room, the bell for that room shakes and rings.

You learn to sleep through every bell but your own. The cook does not hear the library bell. The butler does not hear the nursery. But I hear Mrs. G's room bell in my sleep, even on my afternoon off, even when I am miles away. When I am an old woman and have a house of my own, I am going to have no bells in it at all.

tales.title: From County Mayo
text: I came from County Mayo when I was seventeen, with my passage paid by my aunt who was in service in Chicago already. She met me at the station and the next day took me round the houses on Prairie Avenue, ringing at the back doors, until a housekeeper took me on as a kitchen maid.

Now I am a house maid in a great house, and I send four dollars home every month to my mother, and my little brother is coming over next spring on money I saved. Half the girls on this street are Irish, and the other half are Swedish or Norwegian or German. Go and find Maggie Fitzsimmons at Mr. Field's. She is from the next county to mine, and she knows every Irish girl on the Avenue.

tales.title: Swedish girls
text: The ladies of Prairie Avenue all want a Swedish girl. They say we are clean and honest and do not drink and do not argue. I do not drink. I am honest. I am clean. I argue a great deal, but only in Swedish, so the ladies do not know.

I came from Småland with my sister. She is a cook on Calumet Avenue and I am a parlour maid here. On Sundays we go to the Swedish church and sing the old hymns and eat with people from home. Then we come back to our employers' houses and become quiet and clean and honest again until Thursday.

tales.title: The fire at the Iroquois
text: Last December, just after Christmas, the new Iroquois Theatre downtown caught fire during the matinee. It was full of women and children on their holidays, two thousand people, watching Eddie Foy in Mr. Bluebeard. A light set fire to the curtain, and the fire curtain that was supposed to come down stuck halfway, and the doors opened inward, and some of them were locked.

Six hundred people died in a quarter of an hour. Children, mostly, and their mothers and nurses and maids who had taken them. I knew a girl who was a nursemaid in a house on Michigan Avenue. She took the two children. None of them came home. I still cannot pass a theatre without counting the doors.

tales.title: The back stairs
text: There are two staircases in this house. The family uses the front stairs, wide and carved and carpeted, with a window of coloured glass at the turn. We use the back stairs, narrow and steep and bare, that go from the kitchen to the attic without ever passing through a room where the family might see us.

I go up and down those stairs forty times a day with coal, hot water, trays, linen, slops. My legs are like a soldier's. The family hardly ever sees us working. That is the idea. A well-run house, the housekeeper says, should seem to run itself. As if the coal walked up the stairs on its own.

tales.title: Four dollars a week
text: I am paid four dollars a week and my keep, and that is a good wage for a house maid. In a factory I would get more, maybe six, but I would have to pay for my room and my food, and work in the noise and the dirt, and walk home through the streets at night.

Here I have a room of my own in the attic, with a bed and a washstand and a window that looks out over the roofs to the lake. I eat what the family eats, the next day. I have a uniform. I save almost everything. In five years I will have enough to marry, or to open a little shop, or to go home and buy my father's farm. I have not decided which.

tales.title: Polishing the silver
text: Every Monday the silver is polished, every piece, whether it was used or not. Forks, spoons, knives, ladles, the tea service, the candlesticks, the great centrepiece shaped like a ship. It takes two of us all morning, with rouge and chamois and soft brushes for the engraving.

The butler counts every piece before and after. He has a book with every item listed and its weight. Once a fish fork went missing for three days and the whole household was in an uproar. It turned up in the garbage, where a kitchen girl had thrown it out with the bones. She nearly lost her place. The fork was worth less than a day of her wages.

tales.title: A ladies' maid
text: A ladies' maid is the highest of the maids. I dress my mistress, do her hair, mend her clothes, pack her trunks, and travel with her when she goes away. I know every dress she owns and which gloves go with it. I know her moods before she does.

It is a lonely job. The other servants think I am too grand for them, and the family thinks I am a servant. I sit with neither at dinner. But I have been to New York and to Paris with my mistress, and I have seen the sea, and the Alps from a train window. Go and find Frances Jordan at Mrs. Armour's. She is a ladies' maid too. We are the only two on the Avenue who understand each other.

tales.title: The telephone
text: There is a telephone in this house, on the wall in the back hall, and I am the one who answers it. You lift the ear piece and turn the crank and say: Residence of so-and-so, and then a voice comes out of the wall from somewhere miles away.

The first time it rang I nearly dropped the tray I was carrying. Now I am used to it. I take the messages and write them down and bring them to the mistress on a little silver plate. My mother in Norway has never seen a telephone. When I wrote and told her about it she wrote back that I should go to church more.

tales.title: The ice man
text: The ice man comes three times a week in summer with his wagon full of great blocks cut from the lakes up north in the winter and stored in sawdust. He carries them in on his back with tongs, a hundred pounds at a time, and puts them in the ice box in the pantry.

He is a big Bohemian with a moustache, and every girl on the Avenue knows his name, and he knows all of ours. He winks at the kitchen maids and slips the little children chips of ice to suck. Cook says he is a scoundrel. Cook gives him a cup of coffee and a slice of cake every time he comes.

tales.title: A society wedding
text: When a daughter of one of the great houses is married, the whole Avenue knows it weeks ahead. The dressmakers come and go, the florists, the caterers. On the day, the carriages line the street from Sixteenth to Twenty-second, and the police come to keep the crowds back.

The maids from every house watch from the back windows. We see the bride come out in her white satin and her veil, and we see the guests in their silks, and we make our comments, which are not polite. Then we go back to work. The next morning we hear everything from the girls who served at the wedding breakfast: who drank too much, who cried, who was not invited.

tales.title: My sweetheart drives a wagon
text: My sweetheart drives a delivery wagon for a grocer on Cottage Grove, and he comes to the back door of this house three times a week with the order. We have exactly as long as it takes him to carry in the boxes to talk. Two minutes. Sometimes three, if Cook is in a good mood.

We have been walking out for a year, on my Thursdays. He is saving for a little flat on the West Side. When he has enough, we will marry, and I will leave service. The mistress will be cross. She says she cannot find good girls any more. I say, then she should not let them meet the grocer's boy.

tales.title: The soot
text: Chicago is the dirtiest city in the world. The soot from the railroads and the factories and the furnaces of every house comes down like black snow, all year round. You dust a room in the morning and by evening there is a grey film on every table.

The windows have to be washed every week, inside and out. The lace curtains have to be taken down and washed every month. The white collars of the gentlemen go grey in an afternoon. The lake wind helps a little. When the wind is from the west, from the stockyards, you shut every window in the house and pray.

tales.title: My room under the roof
text: My room is on the top floor, under the roof, with the other maids. It is hot in summer and cold in winter, and the roof slopes down so that I can only stand up straight in the middle. There is a bed, a chair, a washstand, a hook for my clothes, and a little window.

From the window I can see the lake. In the morning, before the bell, I watch the sun come up over the water, all pink and gold, with the ore boats and the schooners going out. Nobody else in the house sees it. They are all asleep. It is the only thing in this house that is entirely mine.

tales.title: The kitchen at five in the morning
text: I am in the kitchen at five, before anybody. I shake down the range and get the fire roaring, and set the kettle on, and start the bread. By six the kitchen maid comes down and starts on the vegetables. By seven the servants' breakfast is on the table and the family's is on the dumbwaiter.

Then it is lunch, and then tea, and then dinner, seven courses if there are guests, and the dishes, and the next day's bread set to rise. I go to bed at ten. I have been a cook for twenty-two years. My feet hurt every minute of every day. But I make the best clear soup in Chicago, and every lady on this street knows it.

tales.title: A dinner for twenty-four
text: Last month we gave a dinner for twenty-four. Oysters, clear turtle soup, a whole salmon on ice, saddle of mutton, roast duck, an ice in the middle to clear the mouth, a salad, a cold bombe, cheese, fruit, coffee. Nine wines. Every plate changed at every course. Forty-eight hands to serve and clear.

We were up until three in the morning washing up. The next day the mistress came down to the kitchen and told Cook it was the finest dinner she had given in years. Cook said thank you, ma'am, very calm. When the mistress went upstairs, Cook sat down at the kitchen table and cried for a minute. Then she got up and started the bread.

tales.title: Going to the market
text: On Tuesdays and Fridays I go to the South Water Street market with the coachman to choose the meat and the fish and the vegetables myself. I do not trust the grocer's boy. He would bring me a fish that died last week and tell me it was this morning's.

South Water Street is the busiest place in Chicago at six in the morning: wagons from every farm in Illinois, crates of chickens, barrels of apples, men shouting in ten languages. I walk through it all like a general, pinching the peaches and smelling the fish, and the commission men know me by name and give me the best. They know if they cheat me I will tell every cook on Prairie Avenue.

tales.title: A German cook
text: I learned to cook in Bavaria, in a hotel kitchen, when I was fourteen. I came to Chicago twenty years ago and I have cooked for three families on this street. They want French food for their dinners and German food for their own lunches, though they would never say so.

So I make them a sauce béarnaise and a soufflé for the guests, and for the family on Sunday a pot roast with dumplings and red cabbage, and the master eats three helpings and says it is the best thing he has eaten all week. The French chefs downtown think they are the only cooks in Chicago. They should taste my strudel.

tales.title: When the family goes away
text: In the summer the family goes away, to the lake shore in Wisconsin or to the East, for July and August, and the house is shut up with the furniture under sheets. Most of the servants go too. One or two of us stay, to keep the house aired and the burglars away.

I stayed last summer. It was the strangest feeling, to have the great house all to myself. I sat in the master's chair in the library one evening, just to see what it felt like. It felt like nothing. It is only a chair. I went back to the kitchen. That is where I am comfortable.

tales.title: Meat from the yards
text: Every piece of meat in this house comes from the stockyards, four miles south and west, where they kill more cattle and hogs in a day than there are people in some towns. When the wind is from the west you can smell it here on Prairie Avenue, a thick sweet smell that gets into the curtains.

The men who own those yards live on this street: Armour, and the others. They made their fortunes from that smell. I have a cousin who works on the killing floor at Armour's. He works ten hours a day standing in blood, for a dollar seventy-five. Then he comes to visit me, and I give him a piece of the roast that his own hands killed. He says it tastes better here.

tales.title: Boiling the water
text: Two summers ago the typhoid came through the city and many people died, mostly in the poor wards on the West Side, but some here too. The doctors said it was in the water. Ever since, I boil every drop that is drunk in this house, and I make the maids boil the water for the babies' bottles too.

They reversed the river four years ago, so the sewage would go down the canal toward St. Louis instead of out into the lake where the city drinks. It helps. St. Louis is very angry about it. I do not care what St. Louis thinks. I care that nobody in this house gets the typhoid.

tales.title: Washday
text: Monday is washday, every week of my life. I start at five with the copper boiler on the laundry stove in the basement. Sheets, tablecloths, napkins, shirts, collars, petticoats, the children's things, the servants' aprons. I boil them, scrub them on the board, rinse them twice, blue them, starch them, wring them through the mangle, and hang them in the drying yard or, if it rains, in the drying room by the furnace.

Tuesday I iron. Wednesday I mend. Thursday I do the fine things, the laces and the silks, by hand. Friday I start getting ready for Monday. My hands are red and cracked from the lye and the hot water, and they will be until I die. But my sheets are the whitest on Prairie Avenue. Ask anybody.

tales.title: The gentleman's collars
text: A gentleman on this street changes his collar twice a day and his shirt once, and every collar must be starched so stiff it could stand up by itself, and ironed until it shines like porcelain. A collar with a crease in it is a disgrace, the butler says, to the whole household.

I iron forty collars a week. I can do one in a minute and a half. My iron is heated on the stove, three of them, so one is always hot while I use the other. I have burned my fingers so many times they no longer feel it. The gentleman has no idea who irons his collars. He has never once come down to the laundry.

tales.title: The laundry in the basement
text: The laundry is in the basement, under the kitchen, where the family never goes. There is a window up high, at the level of the yard, and through it I can see the boots of the coachmen going by, and the wheels of the carriages, and the dogs. That is my view of Prairie Avenue: the ankles of the rich.

But I sing while I work, the songs from home, and the cook upstairs says she can hear me through the floor and it makes the bread rise. Go and find Karolina Hall at Mr. Field's. She is a laundress too, and she sings better than I do. Do not tell her I said so.

tales.title: The horses come first
text: A coachman's day begins in the stable, before light. The horses must be fed, watered, groomed, their feet picked out, their coats brushed until they shine. Then the harness, every buckle polished, every strap oiled. Then the carriage, washed, the brass rubbed, the wheels greased. Then, and only then, my own breakfast.

The family thinks a coachman's job is to sit up on the box in his livery and drive. That is the least of it. A coachman lives for his horses. I know mine better than I know my own children. I know when they are off their feed, when they are lame, when they are in a mood. A good horse is a good friend. A bad horse is a bad master.

tales.title: The automobile
text: A gentleman down the Avenue has bought an automobile, and a man to drive it. It makes a noise like a threshing machine and smells like a lamp and frightens every horse on the Avenue. My mares shied at it last week and nearly put me in the gutter.

The young gentlemen think it is the future. They say in ten years there will be no horses in Chicago at all. I do not believe it. A machine cannot know its way home in the fog. A machine cannot tell when the ice is bad. A machine does not come when you whistle. But I have been teaching myself how the engine works, from a book. Just in case.

tales.title: The livery
text: My livery is dark green, with brass buttons that have the family's initial on them, a high collar, white breeches, black boots to the knee, and a silk hat with a cockade. In winter there is a great caped coat over it. I look like a general.

I hate it. It is hot in summer and the boots pinch and the hat blows off in the lake wind. But I wear it, and I sit up straight on the box, because when the carriage goes down Michigan Avenue on a Sunday afternoon, everybody looks, and they see the family's horses and the family's carriage and the family's coachman, and they know whose they are. That is what the livery is for.

tales.title: Living over the stable
text: The coachman and the groom live over the stable, in rooms above the carriage house at the back of the lot, off the alley. It smells of horse, and hay, and harness oil. I would not trade it for the finest room in the house.

Out here nobody rings a bell for me. I can smoke my pipe, and play my concertina, and have a glass of beer with the coachman from next door. We sit on the bench by the stable door in the evening and talk about horses and the families and the price of oats. It is a whole other street, the alley. The rich live on the front, and we live on the back.

tales.title: The stable boy
text: I started as a stable boy when I was twelve, mucking out and carrying water and sleeping in the hay loft. I am a groom now. One day I will be a coachman, with my own livery and my own horses to drive, and a stable boy of my own to shout at.

There is a groom at the Pullman house, Sam Whatter, who is the best I know with a difficult horse. He can calm a bolting mare just by talking to her. Go and find him at the Pullman stable. Ask him about the grey mare that nobody could ride. He will tell you how he did it. It took him three months and a great many apples.

tales.title: A drive in the park
text: On fine afternoons I drive the mistress out to Washington Park or down the boulevards. The boulevards are wide and smooth, with trees on either side, and every fine carriage in Chicago is out on them, the ladies in their hats and the gentlemen nodding to each other, and the coachmen sizing each other up.

We coachmen have our own races. Not real races, of course, the ladies would faint. But if you can pass another carriage on the boulevard without seeming to try, with your horses stepping high and not breaking stride, that is a victory, and every coachman on the boulevard knows it. I passed the Kimball carriage last Tuesday. I have not stopped smiling since.

tales.title: The night of the Great Fire
text: I was a boy of fourteen in October of 1871, working in a livery stable on the West Side, when the fire started in a barn not far from us. By midnight the whole sky was red. The wind carried the fire across the river and through the business district and up into the North Side, and it burned for two days.

We let all the horses out of the stable and drove them ahead of the fire like cattle, through the streets full of people running with their bundles and their children. I saw a man pushing a piano down the street. I saw a woman carrying a birdcage with no bird in it. When it was over, the heart of the city was gone. And they built it all back, bigger, in a few years. That is Chicago.

tales.title: The car barn bandits
text: Last summer four young men robbed the streetcar company's barn on the South Side and shot two men dead for the payroll. They were hardly older than boys. They hid in a dugout in the sand dunes of Indiana, and when the police came for them there was a gun battle in the dunes.

They hanged three of them this April, at the jail on the North Side. I went to see the crowd outside, though I did not go in. Thousands of people, all quiet, all waiting. A woman next to me said they were only boys. A man said they were murderers. They were both right. I came home and fed the horses and could not eat my own supper.

tales.title: The butler's pantry
text: The butler is the head of the household below stairs, and I rule it from the butler's pantry, with the silver safe and the wine cellar keys on my chain. I hire and dismiss the footmen. I decant the wine. I answer the door to callers. I know who is at home and who is not at home, which is not the same as who is in the house.

A good butler is invisible and indispensable. The family should never have to ask for anything, because it should be there before they think of it. Go and see Thomas Benson at Mr. Field's. He is the finest butler on Prairie Avenue. He will be very polite to you and tell you absolutely nothing.

tales.title: A gentleman's valet
text: A valet dresses his gentleman, shaves him, lays out his clothes, packs for his journeys, keeps his wardrobe in order and his boots polished. I know my gentleman's collar size, his hat size, his shoe size, his opinions on everything, and the name of every man he has quarrelled with.

Henry Deneke was valet in Mr. Armour's own house, before the old gentleman died three years ago. Go and find him at Mrs. Armour's. He will tell you about Mr. Armour, who was one of the richest men in America, and was up before five and at his desk at the yards by seven, every day of his life.

tales.title: The footman
text: A footman's job is to be tall, to stand still, to open doors, to carry trays, and to ride on the back of the carriage looking as if he were made of wood. I am six feet two inches, which is why I was hired. Height in a footman is worth two dollars a week.

When there is a dinner, I stand behind a chair for three hours without moving, without smiling, without hearing a word anybody says. Afterwards in the servants' hall we tell each other everything we heard. The family thinks we are furniture. Furniture has ears.

tales.title: The steward's books
text: In a great house, somebody has to keep the accounts: the grocer's bill, the butcher's, the coal, the ice, the wages, the repairs. That is the steward. I sit in my little office off the back hall with my ledgers and I know what everything in this house costs, down to the last candle.

Ernest Sibbald keeps the books at Mr. Kimball's across the street. We compare notes sometimes. Go and find him. He will tell you exactly how much a piano company owner spends on asparagus in a year. It is a great deal. More than I earn.

tales.title: Feeding the furnace
text: In the cellar of this house there is a furnace as big as a locomotive, and in winter somebody has to feed it, every four hours, day and night, with coal shovelled from the coal room where the wagons tip it down a chute from the alley. That somebody is me.

The heat goes up through pipes to every room in the house, and the family is warm, and has no idea there is a furnace at all. On a January night, at two in the morning, shovelling coal by the light of a lantern with the wind howling outside, I sometimes think I am the most important man in the house. Nobody else thinks so.

tales.title: The housekeeper's keys
text: I carry the keys of the house on a chain at my waist: the linen room, the china closet, the store room, the wine, the guest rooms, the attic. Nothing goes in or out of this house without my knowledge. The maids answer to me. The cook pretends she does not, and does.

I have been in service for thirty years, starting as a scullery girl in Ireland. Now I run a house with eleven servants. The mistress consults me on everything, though she would never admit it to her friends. Go and see Emma Scott at the Pullman house. She keeps the biggest house on the Avenue. If anyone has more keys than I do, it is she.

tales.title: The new girl
text: A new girl came to us last month, from Galway, sixteen years old, straight off the train. She had never seen an electric light, or a flush toilet, or a gas range, or a staircase with a carpet. She stood in the front hall with her mouth open, and then she burst into tears.

I took her down to the kitchen and gave her tea and told her I was just the same, thirty years ago, in a big house in Dublin. Now she is the quickest girl I have. She laughs all day and sings in the scullery and the cook adores her. In ten years she will be a housekeeper herself. Or married. They always get married.

tales.title: The nursery floor
text: The children of this house live on the nursery floor, with me. They sleep there, they eat there, they have their lessons there, and they see their mother for an hour in the afternoon, washed and brushed and dressed in their best, in the drawing room.

So I am the one who knows them. I know which one is afraid of the dark and which one bites his nails and which one is going to be a great lady one day. I taught them to walk and to say their prayers. When they are grown, I suppose, they will forget me. Children always do. But I will not forget them.

tales.title: Walking out with the children
text: Every fine morning I take the children out, the baby in the perambulator and the older ones walking beside, down the Avenue to the lake front or over to the park. All the nurses on the Avenue do the same, so it is like a parade: six nursemaids, twelve children, three dogs.

We nurses sit on the benches and talk while the children play. We know everything about every family on the street. Who is quarrelling, who is ill, who is going abroad, who has lost money. The ladies would be horrified to know how much we know. Children talk, you see. Children tell their nurses everything.

tales.title: The governess
text: I am a governess. I teach the girls of this house French, music, drawing, deportment, and a little arithmetic, though not too much, because their mother thinks too much arithmetic is unladylike. I was educated at a school in Boston. My father was a minister. We had no money.

So I am neither a lady nor a servant. I eat with the family when there are no guests, and on a tray in the schoolroom when there are. The servants think I am grand. The family think I am useful. I think I am lonely. But the youngest girl drew me a picture last week of the two of us, holding hands, under a tree. I have it in my drawer.

tales.title: The scarlet fever
text: When the little boy had scarlet fever last winter, the nursery was shut off from the rest of the house with a sheet soaked in carbolic hung over the door, and I was shut in with him for six weeks. Nobody else could come in. His mother stood outside the sheet every evening and talked to him through it.

The doctor came every day. There was a night when we thought he would die. I sat by his bed and held his hand and sang him every song I knew, twice. In the morning his fever broke. When I came out, after six weeks, the mistress put her arms around me. She has never done that before or since.

glessner_frances_m.title: Monday mornings
text: Ten years ago I began a reading class for the ladies of my acquaintance, on Monday mornings in my library. We meet through the winter. A lady reads aloud, a novel or a history or a book of essays, while the others sew or knit, and then we talk about it, and then we have lunch.

It is the most pleasant morning of my week. Some of the ladies who come are very learned and some are very silly, and the silly ones often say the wisest things. I keep a journal, too, and have since my children were little: what we ate, who came, what was said. My daughter Fanny teases me about it. Go and find her. She will tell you that her mother writes down everything. It is true.

glessner_frances_m.title: Our friend Mr. Thomas
text: Mr. Theodore Thomas has been our friend for many years. When he brought his orchestra here, we were among the people who promised to stand behind it, and for thirteen years we have heard every concert we could, on Friday afternoons and Saturday nights at the Auditorium.

He comes to dinner here, and sits by the fire and talks about Beethoven as if Beethoven were a neighbour he had just been speaking to. He is a hard man, people say, stubborn and proud. He is. He is also the kindest friend we have. This year the city is building him a hall of his own on Michigan Avenue. He has waited a long time for it. I pray he lives long to enjoy it.

glessner_john_j.title: The house that faces inward
text: When we asked Mr. Richardson to build this house, my wife and I wanted something that would turn its back on the noise and the dirt of the street and open toward a sunny court within. He gave us exactly that: granite walls on Prairie Avenue and Eighteenth Street, with small windows like a fortress, and all the light falling into the court behind.

The neighbours were horrified. Mr. Pullman, across the street, said he did not know what he had ever done to have that thing staring him in the face every time he came out of his door. Mr. Richardson never saw it finished. He died before the walls were up. We have lived in it seventeen years now, and I would not change a stone. Go and ask my wife. She chose every chair in it.

glessner_john_j.title: Reapers and mowers
text: I came to Chicago in 1870, a young man from Ohio, to run the western end of our firm, Warder, Bushnell and Glessner, that made reapers and mowers in Springfield. Every farmer from here to Dakota needed a machine to cut his grain, and we sold them by the thousand.

Two years ago our firm and McCormick's and Deering's and the others came together into one company, the International Harvester, and I am a vice president of it. People say we have made a trust. I say we have made a machine within a machine. When I came to Chicago, a man cut his wheat with a cradle, by hand, and his whole family bound the sheaves. Now one man and a team can harvest a field in a day. That is what I am proudest of.

glessner_williamson_martha_l.title: Mrs. Glessner's kitchen
text: I cook for Mr. and Mrs. Glessner, in the kitchen on the north side of the court. Mrs. Glessner is particular. She plans the meals with me every morning, and she writes things down in her book: who came to dinner, and what was said. I think she remembers my dinners better than I do.

When Mr. Thomas the musician comes, I make his favourite things. When the reading class ladies come on Monday, I make the lunch, light, because ladies who have been sitting all morning do not want a heavy lunch. Go and find Mrs. Glessner in the house. If you ask her who came to dinner a year ago, she can tell you. It is all in the book.

pa1904_armour_mrs_philip_d.title: The million dollar sermon
text: Fourteen years ago a young minister named Dr. Gunsaulus preached a sermon called: What I would do with a million dollars. He said he would build a school where the sons and daughters of working people could learn to be engineers and architects and chemists. My husband was in the church that morning. Afterwards he went up to the minister and said: if you will give five years of your life, I will give the million dollars.

So they built the Armour Institute, on the South Side, and there are hundreds of young people there now learning to build bridges and engines. My husband died three years ago, the year after our son Philip. He made his fortune in the stockyards, from meat. People say hard things about the yards, and some of them are true. But the Institute is true, too. Ask Henry Deneke, who looked after him. He will tell you what kind of man he was.

pa1904_field_marshall.title: Give the lady what she wants
text: I came to Chicago in 1856, a young man from the hills of Massachusetts, to clerk in a dry goods store on Lake Street. I slept in the store. I saved half of what I earned. I learned that a customer who is treated honestly will come back, and a customer who is cheated will tell twenty others.

Now the store on State Street is the largest in the world, perhaps, and we are building a new one beside it, bigger still. I am told I am the richest man in Chicago. I do not think about that. I think about whether the lady who came in this morning for a spool of thread got it quickly and was treated well. That is the business. The rest is just arithmetic.

pa1904_field_marshall.title: The store burned
text: In October of 1871 our store on State Street was the finest in the city, a marble palace. On the second night of the fire it burned to the ground with everything in it. We saved what goods we could, in wagons, and carried them to the lake shore. When it was over, I stood in the ashes with my partner and we looked at each other.

Two weeks later we opened again, in a horse car barn at State and Twentieth Street, with planks on barrels for counters. The ladies of Chicago came in their old clothes, because their good ones had burned, and bought new ones from us. We were rebuilt within two years. A fire can take a building. It cannot take a name. Ask my butler, Benson, what he thinks of fire. He has opinions.

pa1904_jones_fernando.title: I came in 1835
text: I came to Chicago in 1835, a boy of fifteen, with my father. It was a town of a few hundred people, frame houses and log cabins in the mud along the river, and the old fort, and the Potawatomi camped on the prairie. That summer the great land craze was on, and every man in Chicago was buying and selling lots that were under water half the year.

I learned to speak a little of the Potawatomi language, trading with them. That autumn they gathered for the last time and went away west across the Mississippi, as the treaty said. I watched them go. Now I live on Prairie Avenue in a house of stone, on land that was open prairie when I was a boy, with wolves on it. I am one of the last who remember. When I am gone, nobody will.

pa1904_kimball_william_w.title: A piano in every parlour
text: I came to Chicago from Maine in 1857, with almost nothing, and started selling pianos and organs that other men made. People said nobody on the prairie would buy a piano. They were wrong. Every farm family that had a little money wanted an organ in the parlour, so that the daughters could play hymns on Sunday.

Then I started making them myself, organs first and then pianos, in a great factory on the West Side. The Kimball organ is in churches all over the country now. My wife and I built this house twelve years ago, like a French château, with a gallery for her paintings. Go and see Ernest Sibbald, who keeps our accounts. He will tell you how many pianos we sold last year. I would rather not boast.

pa1904_lee_blewett.title: The general's son
text: My father is General Stephen D. Lee, who commanded an army corps for the South in the war, and was at Vicksburg and Atlanta and Nashville. I grew up in Mississippi, in the years after the war, when we had nothing but our name. I studied law at Harvard and abroad, and came north to work for the Illinois Central Railroad, which runs from here all the way down to my father's country.

So I am a Southerner in a Northern city, married to a Northern lady, the daughter of a man who made machines for Northern farms. My father fought the men whose sons I dine with. None of us mention it. When the old soldiers march on Decoration Day, I stand on the sidewalk with my hat in my hand, like everyone else, and think of my father.

pa1904_lee_frances_glessner.title: My brother went to Harvard
text: My brother George went to Harvard. I wanted to go too, and I was not allowed. Young ladies of good family did not go to college, my parents thought, or not to Harvard, which does not take them in any case. So I was taught at home, in the schoolroom on the top floor of my father's house, with George, until he left for Cambridge and I stayed.

I have a husband now, Mr. Blewett Lee, and three children. I read everything I can. I am interested in how things work, how they are made, how a house is put together down to the last nail. My mother says that is not a subject for a lady. My husband is a lawyer. Go and find him. He has very decided views on what is a subject for a lady.

pa1904_lowden_frank_orren.title: Seventy-nine ballots
text: This spring I ran for governor of Illinois. The Republican convention met at Springfield in May, and there were seven of us wanting the nomination, and nobody had a majority, and nobody would give way. They voted, and voted again, and again, for three weeks. Every night we bargained in hotel rooms full of cigar smoke until two in the morning.

On the seventy-ninth ballot they gave it to Charles Deneen. I lost. I went to Deneen and shook his hand and promised to work for him, and I will. I grew up on a farm in Iowa and taught school and read law by lamplight. A man who has lost one fight has learned how the fight is fought. I am not done. Not by a long way.

pa1904_lowden_mrs_frank_orren.title: The hotel named for me
text: When my father built his town at Pullman, he named the hotel there after me: the Hotel Florence. I was a girl of thirteen. I used to go down on his private car and walk through the halls and see my name on the menus. It was the proudest I have ever been.

My father thought of everything for that town except what the people in it wanted. I have thought about that a great deal since he died. I married a lawyer from a farm in Iowa, who taught school to pay for his own education, and who has never let me forget what it means to work for a living. Go and find him. He has just lost his first election, and he is taking it very well. Mostly.

pa1904_meeker_arthur.title: The packing business
text: I went to work for Mr. Philip Armour when I was a young man, and I have been in the packing business ever since. Every day the trains bring in cattle and hogs and sheep from the whole West, and every day we kill them and dress them and pack them and send them out in refrigerator cars to every city in the country, and to Europe.

People are horrified by the yards. I understand that. It is a hard business, and a bloody one, and the smell is terrible. But a working man in New York can eat beef for supper today because of what we do in Chicago. My daughters do not understand what I do. I do not take them to the yards. One day, perhaps, I will.

pa1904_pullman_mrs_george_m.title: My husband's sleeping cars
text: My husband, George Pullman, built a railway car that a man could sleep in, with beds that folded out of the walls and linen and porters, so that a traveller could go to sleep in Chicago and wake up in New York. Before him, people sat up all night on wooden benches. He made a fortune from that idea, and he built a whole town south of the city, with brick houses and a church and a library, for the men who made his cars.

Then came the strike, ten years ago. The men he had built a town for turned against him. I do not think he ever understood why. He died three years later. My daughter Florence lives near me now with her husband and her children. Go and find her. She was always her father's favourite. The hotel in his town bears her name.

pa1904_pullman_mrs_george_m.title: The grave at Graceland
text: When my husband died, seven years ago, there were people who hated him very much: men who had been in the strike, and their friends. We were afraid of what they might do. So he was buried at Graceland in a pit lined with concrete, in a lead coffin, and over the coffin they laid steel rails and more concrete, tons of it, so that no one could ever disturb him.

The newspapers said it was to keep the strikers away. It was. It was also because he was a man who always planned for everything, even this. I visit him on Sundays. There is a tall column there, very handsome. Nobody can tell from looking at it that he lies under a fortress of his own making.

pa1904_shortall_john_g.title: The night I saved the books
text: On the night of the great fire, in October of 1871, every record of every piece of land in Chicago was in the courthouse, and the courthouse burned. Every deed, every mortgage, every title, gone. But my firm kept our own abstracts of title, copies of all the records, in our office. And the fire was coming.

I found a wagon in the street, and its driver did not want to go anywhere near the fire, and I persuaded him. Some say at the point of a pistol. I will not say. We loaded the books and drove them out ahead of the flames. Two other firms saved theirs too. Afterwards the legislature made our books the lawful record, and every title in Chicago rests on them today. Go and find Fernando Jones. He was in the same business. He will tell you whether I really had a pistol.

pa1904_shortall_john_g.title: The Humane Society
text: For many years I have been president of the Illinois Humane Society. We began by protecting horses, because the horses of this city are beaten and starved and worked until they drop in the street. Then we began to protect children, because, God help us, children in this city are treated worse than the horses.

We have agents who go into the tenements and the stables and the factories. We have put drinking fountains for horses on the street corners. We take children away from fathers who beat them. Some people say it is none of our business. I say it is everybody's business. A city is judged by how it treats the creatures that cannot speak for themselves.

pa1904_wood_casey_a.title: The eye doctor
text: I am a doctor of the eye. I came to Chicago from Canada by way of Europe, where I studied in the great eye hospitals of London and Vienna and Berlin. Every day in my office men and women come to me afraid of going blind, and some of them I can help, and some I cannot.

The eye is the most beautiful thing in the body, I think. When you look into it with the ophthalmoscope, with the little light, you see the blood vessels branching like the roots of a tree, and the nerve where the world comes in. When I am not in my office, I am watching birds. Every creature sees the world differently. I would like to know how.

asks.q: What time do you start in the morning?
a: Half past five, before the family stirs. Fires laid in the grates even in summer for the damp, the front steps scrubbed, the brass on the door polished, the dining room swept and the breakfast table laid, all before eight. Then the bedrooms when the family has gone down, and the stairs, and the silver.

When the family has gone up and the last tray has come down, ten or eleven. Thursday afternoon and every other Sunday are mine. On Thursday the whole Avenue's maids are out on Michigan Avenue at once, in our best hats. The mistresses on the Avenue have no idea how much we know about each other's houses.

more.q: What do you do on your afternoon?
a: The Lake Front, if it is fine, or the shops on State Street just to look, or the vaudeville. Since the Iroquois burned last December, none of us goes near a big theatre. I go to the park and sit by the water and do nothing at all, which is the finest thing in the world.

asks.q: Did you hear about the Iroquois Theatre fire?
a: Everyone in Chicago knows somebody. It was the thirtieth of December, a matinee, the house packed with mothers and children for the Christmas pantomime, when the scenery caught fire and the curtain did not come down and the doors opened inwards. Six hundred people died in a quarter of an hour. Mostly women and children.

A girl who was in service two houses down took her mistress's children. They came home. She did not; she went back in for the youngest and the crowd took her. Her mistress paid for the funeral. I still pass the house and look up at the window where she used to sit.
