Every theatre in the city was shut while the inspectors went round, and they have found exits nailed shut and no water in the pipes and fire curtains made of nothing. Mr. Shortall of the Humane Society has made the children of this city his work for years. Ask him what has been done since. He will tell you not enough.

asks.q: How do you know when you are wanted?
a: The bells. There is a board in the servants' hall with a little flag or a bell for every room, and when the mistress pulls the cord in the library, the library bell rings and its flag drops. In the newer houses there are speaking tubes, and now the telephone. But the bells are what I hear in my sleep.
When somebody is ill, or wants a hot drink, or has heard a noise. The master's bell is the one we fear. Two short rings means come at once. One long means he has lost his spectacles again.

asks.q: Where are you from?
a: County Mayo, by way of Queenstown and New York, six years ago. My aunt was in service on the North Side and she found me my first place. Now there are four of us from the same parish on Prairie Avenue, and the cook in the house across the street is my second cousin.

Every month, to my mother, by the money order at the post office. Three dollars of my sixteen. My brother is coming over next spring, I hope, and I am saving for his passage. He wants to be a policeman. Half the police in Chicago are from Mayo, so he may manage it.
Every Sunday morning, the early Mass, before the family wakes. Then I come back and serve the family breakfast before they go to their own church. God gets me first.

asks.q: Is it hard to learn English?
a: Very hard, at first. I came from Småland four years ago and I knew only yes and thank you. The mistress spoke to me slowly, as if I were deaf, and pointed at things. Now I can read the newspaper. The cook is Irish and laughs at my words, and I laugh at hers.

On the North Side, a whole city of Swedes: churches, shops, newspapers in Swedish, dances on Saturday. On Prairie Avenue the girls are Irish and Swedish and German and Norwegian, and we talk to each other in a sort of English that nobody upstairs could follow.

asks.q: What's the house at the corner of Eighteenth like?
a: The Glessner house? Like a castle that turned its back on the street. From the Avenue it is all granite and small windows, and the girls who go by say it must be very dark inside. It is not. Everything opens onto the court behind, full of light and ivy. It is the strangest house on the Avenue and the best to work in, they say.

The cook, Mattie Williamson, who knows the mistress's book of dinners better than the mistress does. The maids. The men in the stable. Mrs. Glessner writes everything in her journal, the girls say: who came, who said what, what was eaten. Go and ask Mattie what Mr. Thomas the musician likes for dinner.

asks.q: Is it good money, service on the Avenue?
a: Four dollars a week for a housemaid with her room and board. A cook gets more, six or seven. A butler more again. A girl in a factory gets as much, but she pays her own rent and her own dinner, and she breathes the factory all day. Here at least the air is the lake's.

more.q: Would you rather work in a shop?
a: At Field's? The shop girls stand all day and have their wages docked if they are a penny short. But they go home at night and nobody rings for them. Some days I envy them. Most days I eat better than they do.

asks.q: Where do the servants sleep?
a: At the top of the house, in the little rooms under the roof, two to a room, hot in summer and cold in winter. We go up and down by the back stairs, never the front, and we are never to be seen on the front stairs except to clean them, before the family wakes.

A bed, a washstand, a chair, a chest of drawers, a picture of the Sacred Heart and a photograph of my mother. The window looks over the alley to the carriage houses. On summer nights I can hear the horses moving in their stalls, and the trains on the lakefront, and nothing else.

asks.q: Are you going to the World's Fair at St. Louis?
a: Everybody wants to go. It opened in April for the Louisiana Purchase, a hundred years of it, and they say it is bigger than our own Fair of ninety-three. A palace of electricity, a giant bird cage, and Mr. Ferris's own wheel from our Fair, carried down and set up again, and people from the whole world in villages you can walk through.

Some of the families on the Avenue went down in May in their private cars. The servants who went came back with picture postcards and stories about ice cream served in a rolled waffle, which you eat cone and all. Mr. Kimball took prizes for his pianos at our own Fair in ninety-three. Ask him if he has sent any to St. Louis.

more.q: Do you remember the Fair of ninety-three?
a: The White City! I was a girl and I went three times. The lights at night on the lagoon were like nothing in the world. Everybody in Chicago says St. Louis will never match it. People from St. Louis say otherwise. They would.

asks.q: How long does it take to clean the silver?
a: A whole morning every week, two of us, with whiting and ammonia and soft cloths, in the butler's pantry with the door shut. Forks, spoons, salvers, candlesticks, the tea service, the epergne for the centre of the table. Every piece is counted out and counted back.

Not in this house. In a house two doors down, last year, a spoon was missed, and a girl was turned off without a character. The spoon was found in the soup tureen a month later. Nobody went to tell the girl. I think about her.

asks.q: Does the house have a telephone?
a: In the back hall, on the wall, with a crank and a little earpiece on a cord. The master uses it to call his office and the mistress to call the grocer. I answer it. You say the number of the house and then wait while somebody shouts at you from the other end. I was frightened of it for a month.

The young ladies, calling each other about dances. Their mother says it is not ladylike to speak on the telephone. They do it anyway, in the back hall, in whispers, and I am to say they are out if their mother asks.

asks.q: What's for dinner tonight?
a: A clear soup, a fish, a joint of lamb with new peas, a salad and a lemon ice, for six, with the master's brother and his wife. The fish came from the market on South Water Street at six this morning on the grocer's wagon. The ice is in the box. The peas the scullery maid is shelling now, and eating one in three.

A chicken pie that the master asks for every Sunday and is not supposed to have, because the doctor says he is too stout. On Sunday I make it anyway. The mistress pretends not to notice. Upstairs is full of things everyone pretends not to notice.

more.q: Do you have a gas range?
a: A big coal range, and a gas stove beside it for quick things, which the mistress had put in last year. I was afraid of it at first. Now I would not give it up. The coal range takes an hour to come up; the gas comes up with a match.

asks.q: How do you keep food cold in summer?
a: The ice box, an oak chest lined with zinc, with a block of lake ice in the top that the ice man brings every morning, a hundred pounds on his back with tongs. The cold falls down onto the butter and the milk and the meat. The water drips into a pan that the scullery maid empties, if she remembers.

more.q: Where does the ice come from?
a: From the lakes and ponds north of the city, cut in the winter in great blocks and stored in ice houses packed in sawdust. In July the ice man is the most popular man on the Avenue. The children follow his wagon for the chips.

asks.q: Where do you buy food?
a: The grocer and the butcher come to the back door every morning for the order, and deliver by noon. For fish and fruit and the best vegetables I go to the South Water Street market myself once a week, early, with the coachman to drive me. It is a mile of wagons and shouting and crates and horses.

Of course. The market men know me and I know them. A cook who pays the first price is a cook who does not care for her master's money, and he hears of it. A cook who drives a hard bargain is a cook the market respects.

asks.q: What's the biggest dinner you've ever cooked?
a: Twenty-four, for a dinner after the opera, with nine courses, oysters to ices. I had three girls extra for the day and a man from the caterer's for the ices. We started at six in the morning. The last plates came down at one. I sat on the back stairs and could not lift my arms.

Half the Avenue and some men from the orchestra. Mr. Thomas the conductor was one. He came down to the kitchen afterwards to thank me himself, which no guest had ever done. I have been his servant ever since, in my heart.

asks.q: How many horses do you keep?
a: Six in the stable behind the house: two pairs of carriage horses, bays, matched to the hair, a cob for the light trap, and the master's saddle horse that he does not ride as often as he should. I feed them at five, groom them by seven, and harness by nine for the master's drive to his office.

A brougham for the master in town, a victoria for the mistress on fine afternoons in the park, and a big closed carriage for the opera and the theatre. Each has its own harness and its own lamps, and every bit of brass must shine like a mirror. A dirty carriage is the coachman's shame.

There are a few now on Michigan Avenue, smelling and banging and frightening the horses. One of the young men on the Avenue has one. The horses hate them, and so do I. The master says they are a fad. I hope he is right. A motor car needs a mechanic, not a coachman.

asks.q: Where do you live?
a: Over the carriage house, behind the main house, with my wife and two children, in four rooms over the stalls. Warm in winter from the horses below, and on summer nights the smell comes up through the floor. My boys go to sleep to the sound of the horses chewing. They think it is the best sound in the world.

more.q: Do the families' coachmen know each other?
a: We are a club. Every carriage house along the alley has a coachman, and we stand in the alley in the evening, smoking, and talk about horses and masters. We know whose horse is lame, whose groom drinks, and whose master is going broke before his banker does.

asks.q: Where's the nicest drive in Chicago?
a: Along the lake on the boulevards, out to Washington Park and Jackson Park, where the Fair was. On a summer afternoon every carriage on the Avenue is out there, the ladies in their summer gowns, the coachmen in their summer livery, all going at a walk so everybody can see everybody else.

Mr. Field's, of course: a pair of blacks that cost more than my house. But Mr. Field himself prefers to walk to his store every morning, three miles, in all weathers. A man with the finest horses in Chicago who walks. That is a man who knows what he is.

asks.q: What's the worst part of the job?
a: Waiting. Outside the opera, outside a dinner, outside a ball, in January, on the box, with a buffalo robe and a lantern, until two in the morning. The horses stand with their blankets on and their breath smoking and I stand with them. You get to know a horse well on those nights.

Driving a pair of good horses fast on the lake shore on a crisp morning, with the sun coming up out of the water, and nobody in the carriage at all because I am exercising them. Then the horses and I are the masters of the Avenue.

asks.q: How did you learn about horses?
a: On my father's farm in Kerry, and then as a stable boy for an English family in Dublin, and then in the livery stables of New York, and then here. Twenty years of horses. I can tell a horse's age by its teeth and its temper by its ears, and a bad groom by the horse's coat.

more.q: What makes a good carriage horse?
a: Steady nerves above all. A carriage horse in Chicago must stand still for cable cars, elevated trains, fire engines, brass bands and the motor cars. He must go at a walk among a thousand other horses without kicking any of them. A horse like that is worth more than a racehorse.

asks.q: What day is wash day?
a: Monday, every Monday, in the laundry in the basement, with three set tubs, a copper boiler on the range, a wringer, and a drying room with racks for when it rains. The whole house's linen, every sheet, napkin, collar and petticoat. Tuesday is ironing. Wednesday is mending.

From six in the morning to six at night, two of us. The white things boiled, the coloured things in warm water, the woollens in cool, the master's collars starched stiff enough to cut a finger. By evening the steam has taken the curl out of my hair and the skin off my knuckles.

asks.q: How do you iron so many shirts?
a: With six flat irons heating on the stove at once, using one while the others warm. A shirt front takes a quarter of an hour if it is to be done properly, with the starch. The master wears a fresh shirt every day and two on the days he dines out. That is ten shirts a week for him alone.

more.q: Have you seen the new electric irons?
a: In the shop window at Field's. They plug into the wall where the light goes. The mistress says perhaps next year. I say I will believe it when it does not set the house on fire.

asks.q: Whose children do you look after?
a: Two little ones, a boy of four and a girl of two, in the nursery on the third floor. I wake them, wash them, dress them, give them their breakfast, walk them in the park, give them their dinner, put them down for their sleep, and bring them down to the drawing room at five to see their mother for half an hour in their best clothes.
They love her the way you love a beautiful lady who comes to see you. They love me the way you love bread. When the boy falls down, he calls for me. I try not to be proud of that.

To the lake shore, or down the Avenue to the statue at Eighteenth Street, the bronze of the Indian chief saving the lady. The boy asks about it every time and I tell him what the policeman on the corner told me: that it was a battle long ago, when Chicago was a fort, and the chief was a good man.

asks.q: Do you teach the children too?
a: Their letters, their prayers, their manners, a little French. When they are six they will have a governess for lessons, and then school. My job is to make them good children; the governess's will be to make them clever. I think mine is the harder.
They are children. The boy bit his sister on Tuesday and she pulled his hair on Wednesday, and on Thursday they were best friends again. That is not badness. That is practice.

asks.q: What does a housekeeper do?
a: Everything that keeps the house running, and nothing that anyone sees. I keep the keys to the linen, the china, the stores and the wine. I hire and train the maids, order the coal and the soap and the candles, keep the accounts, and see that every room is ready before anyone wants it.

The maids. A good girl is hard to find and harder to keep. She marries, or goes to a better place, or goes back to Ireland to bury her mother. In fifteen years I have trained thirty girls. Some of them are cooks now in houses grander than this one. I count that as my wages.

asks.q: What does a butler do all day?
a: Answer the door, receive the cards, announce the guests, serve the wine, carve at the sideboard, keep the silver, wind the clocks, hire the footmen, see that every man in the house does his work. A good butler is like a good clock: nobody notices him until he stops.

I have announced a Vice-President, three senators, two English lords and the President of the University. And Mr. Pullman, before he died, who walked in as if he owned the house as well. The great ones are easier than the rich ones. The great ones say thank you.

asks.q: What do you do in this house?
a: I am the house man. I shovel coal into the furnace in winter, carry the ashes out, wash the windows, beat the carpets, carry the trunks, mend what breaks, and do whatever heavy work the maids cannot. In summer I wash the house down and paint the iron fence.

A wife and three children in a flat off Twenty-second Street, a half hour's walk. I see them on Sunday. My boy is ten and he wants to work on the railroad. I tell him to stay in school. He says I did not. I say that is why.

asks.q: What line of business are you in?
a: The Board of Trade, mostly: grain, which is to say, I buy wheat that does not yet exist from men who do not own it, and sell it to men who do not want it, and somehow everybody eats. My father did it before me. It is either the most important business in the world or the silliest, depending on the day.

more.q: Who's the most respected man on the Avenue?
a: Glessner at the corner of Eighteenth, for his sense, and Field for his money, and Kimball for his music. Glessner has been in the reaper trade since the war, and two years ago they joined all the reaper companies into the International Harvester and he is on its board. Go and ask him about it. He thinks it a great thing and a sad one.

asks.q: Which club do you belong to?
a: The Chicago Club, on Michigan Avenue, where I lunch every day, and the Union League, where I argue about politics, and the Commercial Club, where I argue about the city. A man in my position belongs to clubs as a ship belongs to harbours: he calls in, takes on news, and goes out again.

more.q: What are they talking about this summer?
a: The convention, Mr. Roosevelt, the war in the Far East between the Japanese and the Russians, which the Japanese are winning against all expectation, and Mr. Burnham's plan for the lake front. And the price of beef, always the price of beef.

asks.q: Is the Avenue still the best address in Chicago?
a: It was for thirty years. Now the young people are moving north, to the Lake Shore Drive, where Mrs. Palmer built her castle. The railroads have come closer, the smoke is worse, and there are boarding houses on Michigan Avenue a few blocks south. But the old families stay. Mr. Field stays. Glessner stays.

Not as it is, I think. Nothing in Chicago lasts as it is. Fernando Jones has lived here since the town was a few hundred people in the mud. Ask him how many times he has seen the best address in Chicago move. He will count them on his fingers.

asks.q: What happened in the great strike ten years ago?
a: The Pullman strike of ninety-four. Mr. Pullman cut wages at his works and would not cut the rents in his town, and the men struck. Then the railway union refused to handle any train with a Pullman car, and the whole country's railroads stopped. The President sent in the army. There was burning in the yards and men were killed.

That depends on which club you ask. I will tell you this: Mr. Pullman thought he was a good father to his workmen, and they thought he was a landlord. Both were partly right. Mrs. Pullman lives at Eighteenth and Prairie still. She does not speak of it. Do not ask her unless she raises it.

asks.q: Do you remember the great fire?
a: I was a young man of twenty in seventy-one. I stood on the lake shore with my mother and my sisters and our silver in a pillowcase, and watched the city burn behind us for two days. The heat was so great that the people waded into the lake. In the morning there was nothing between the river and Fullerton but chimneys.

more.q: How did the city come back so fast?
a: Because everyone who had lost everything had nothing to do but build. The money came from the East and from Europe, the bricks came by the trainload, and in two years you could hardly tell. That is Chicago. It does not mourn. It borrows.

asks.q: Will you buy an automobile?
a: I have been offered one. They say a motor car will go twenty miles an hour on a good road, of which there are about three in Illinois. It needs a mechanic, it frightens the horses, and it smells. I suspect in ten years everyone will have one, and I shall have to give up my coachman.

more.q: Has anyone on the Avenue got one?
a: A few of the young men have, and they race them on the boulevards at dawn and the police chase them on bicycles. George Glessner up the Avenue has read everything about them. Ask him if he thinks they will last.

asks.q: What's become of the old Fair grounds?
a: The University of Chicago stands beside them, on the Midway, grey stone in the English style, a dozen years old and growing every year. Mr. Rockefeller gave the money and Mr. Field gave the land. The Field Museum is in the old Fine Arts building in Jackson Park, full of everything the Fair left behind.

They say it will be the best in the West. Dr. Harper has hired professors from everywhere at double wages. My son goes to Yale, of course. But I am told the young men at Chicago work harder, which may be because they have nothing else to do on the Midway.

asks.q: What good works do you do?
a: The Visiting Nurse Association, the Home for the Friendless, a sewing circle for the Children's Hospital, and every winter a committee for the coal fund. The poor of this city freeze in the winter and boil in the summer, and a lady with time and means must do what she can.

more.q: Have you been to Hull House?
a: Twice, with Miss Addams herself showing us round: the nursery, the kindergarten, the classes for working girls, the gymnasium, the coffee house, all in the middle of the worst of the West Side. It made me ashamed of my drawing room. Mrs. Armour gives to the poor more quietly than anyone on the Avenue. Ask her about her husband's institute.

asks.q: Do you belong to a club?
a: The Fortnightly, which meets in its rooms on Michigan Avenue to hear papers on literature and history; and the Woman's Club, which does good works and argues about the vote. We have the vote for the school board and for the University of Illinois trustees, and nothing else. We are told to be content.
No. But I am patient. Mrs. Glessner has a reading class on Monday mornings in her library that is better than any club, and harder to get into. Go and ask her if there is a vacancy. There never is.

asks.q: Do you go to the orchestra?
a: Every Friday afternoon in the season, at the Auditorium, in our box. Mr. Thomas plays Beethoven and Wagner and the new Germans, and the ladies of Chicago listen in their hats. Some of us understand it. All of us enjoy being seen to.

Mr. Thomas has wanted his own hall for years, smaller than the Auditorium, built for music. The guarantors raised the money last winter and it is going up now on Michigan Avenue across from the Art Institute. They say it will open by Christmas. The Glessners were among the first to give. Ask her about it, and watch her change the subject.

asks.q: Where do you go for the summer?
a: Away, as soon as we can. The city in July is all dust and heat and smoke from the railroads. Some families go to Lake Geneva, some to the north shore, some to Maine or New Hampshire. We go to our cottage at Lake Forest at the end of the week, and the servants close up the house with sheets over everything.

The men, mostly, who come out on the train at the weekend. And a few servants to keep the house, and the coachman with the horses. And the Avenue gets very quiet, and the maids sit on the front steps in the evening when nobody is looking, which they think nobody knows.

asks.q: Where do your gowns come from?
a: The best from Paris, from Worth or Doucet, ordered on our trip abroad every second spring. The rest from Field's dressmaking rooms, which are as good as anything in New York, and cost nearly as much. A lady needs a morning dress, a walking dress, an afternoon dress, a dinner dress and a ball gown, and a different set for each season.

The sleeves are smaller than they were ten years ago, thank heaven, and the skirts are longer and the figures more S-shaped, which is to say the corsets are worse. The young girls play golf and tennis in shirtwaists and short skirts. Their mothers are shocked. Their mothers did the same with bicycles.

asks.q: How many servants do you keep?
a: Eleven: a butler, two footmen, a cook and a kitchen maid, two housemaids, a parlour maid, a laundress, a nurse and the coachman, with a groom in the stable. It sounds a great many until you see the size of the house. A house like this one is a small town, and the servants are its government.

I hope so. I pay fair wages and I give them their afternoons and I do not count the spoons. A girl who is happy in your house stays, and a girl who stays knows your ways. My cook has been with me eleven years. I would sooner lose my husband's business partner.

asks.q: Where do you go to college?
a: Yale, class of nought-six. I am home for the summer. In the autumn it is football, which my mother thinks will kill me, and Greek, which my father thinks will not do me any good. Both may be right. The man I room with is from New York and has never seen a stockyard. I am taking him to see one this week.

more.q: What do you want to do?
a: My father wants me to go into the business. I want to be an architect, like Mr. Burnham or Mr. Sullivan. My father says architects are artists, and artists starve. I said Mr. Burnham does not look as if he starves. That was a mistake.

asks.q: Do you follow the baseball?
a: The Cubs, of course, at the West Side Grounds. Frank Chance at first, Tinker at short and Evers at second. They are going to win the pennant one of these years, everybody says, if the Giants ever lose. My father prefers the White Sox, on the South Side, because they are nearer and because Comiskey once sold him a horse.

more.q: Do you go to the games?
a: Whenever I can get away. You take the elevated to the West Side and sit in the sun with ten thousand men in straw hats, shouting. It is the best afternoon in the world. My mother thinks I am at the library.

asks.q: Do you cycle?
a: Everyone did ten years ago, when the safety bicycle came in: Michigan Avenue on a Sunday morning was a river of wheels. Now it is golf and tennis and motor cars. But I still ride to the lake in the mornings before it is hot. On a bicycle nobody can tell whether you are rich or poor.

The bicycle craze is over. The girls who fought to ride in bloomers are married now and their daughters play tennis in skirts. It always goes like that: the mothers fight, the daughters take it for granted.

asks.q: Have you come out in society yet?
a: Last winter, at a dance my mother gave at the house, with the ballroom on the third floor opened up and the orchestra in the hall. I wore white, of course, with my grandmother's pearls. I danced every dance and broke the heel off my slipper and had to finish in my stockings. Nobody noticed. Everybody noticed.

Calls and teas and dinners and dances, all winter, until somebody suitable proposes. My mother has a list. I have a different list. Neither of us has shown the other. I would rather go to college. My mother says that is what I will say until I fall in love.

asks.q: What do young ladies do for amusement?
a: Golf, at the clubs out in the country, at Wheaton or Lake Forest. Tennis at the Kenwood courts. Riding in the park in the mornings. Theatre parties, now that the theatres have been inspected and opened again. And in the summer, sailing on Lake Geneva, where half of Prairie Avenue goes in July.

more.q: Are you any good at golf?
a: I beat my brother last Saturday by four strokes and he has not spoken to me since. I am taking that as a compliment.

asks.q: Do you think women should have the vote?
a: I do. My mother does not, and my grandmother is furious about it. In Illinois we can vote for the school trustees and nothing else. In Wyoming and Colorado and Utah women vote for everything, and the sky has not fallen. My father says politics would make women coarse. I have heard my father talk politics. I think it would make women bored.
Ladies do not march. Not yet. We sign petitions and go to lectures and argue at dinner. When I am my mother's age, perhaps, we shall march. Perhaps I shall be at the front.

asks.q: Are you excited about the Fourth of July?
a: Three more days! Firecrackers and Roman candles and sparklers, and a parade on Michigan Avenue, and lemonade, and my father takes us to the lake shore at night for the rockets. Last year my brother lit a firecracker in the stable and the horses kicked their stalls. He was not allowed out for a week.
My mother says no. She reads in the paper every year about boys who lost their fingers. My nurse says I may hold a sparkler if she holds my wrist. I am going to hold it myself. Do not tell her.

asks.q: What is the statue at Eighteenth Street?
a: It is an Indian chief stopping another Indian from hurting a lady, and there is a man lying down and a little child. Mr. Pullman put it there, by his house, because that is where the fight was a long time ago, when Chicago was a fort. My nurse says the chief's name was Black Partridge and he was brave.

We are not supposed to climb on it. My brother did once and a policeman shouted. Mrs. Pullman lives in the big house right behind it. She waves at us from the window sometimes. Go and ask her about the statue. She knows the whole story.

asks.q: Have you been to the zoo?
a: To Lincoln Park, on the North Side, on the streetcar with my nurse. There are bears in a pit, a lion that yawns, monkeys that throw things, and a buffalo, a real one. My nurse says there used to be buffalo on the prairie right here. I do not believe it. Where would they go?
The bear. He sits up and begs for peanuts, and when he gets one he looks at you as if to say: is that all? I gave him my whole bag. My nurse was cross. The bear was happy.

asks.q: Do you go to school?
a: To a school for boys on Michigan Avenue, with a master who has a moustache and a ruler. Latin, arithmetic, geography, penmanship. I am bad at penmanship. My letters lean over as if they were tired. In the autumn my sister goes to a school for girls where they learn French and the piano.

Geography. We have a big map of the world and the master puts pins in it for the war in Manchuria. The Japanese are winning. I am for the Japanese because they are smaller. My father says that is a very good reason.

asks.q: What's your favourite treat?
a: Ice cream, from the confectioner's on Twenty-second Street, in a dish with a wafer. My cousin went to the Fair in St. Louis and she says they put it in a cone made of waffle that you eat too. I do not believe her. Who would eat the dish?
My sister has a pony, Buttons, and I have to share him. He bites. He only bites me. My sister says it is because I pull his tail. I only did that once. Ponies remember everything.

asks.q: Who is your best friend in the house?
a: The coachman. He lets me sit on the box and hold the reins in the alley, and he tells me the horses' names and what each one likes to eat. And the cook, who gives me the cake ends. And my nurse, but she is not a friend, she is my nurse. Upstairs my mother is very beautiful and smells of violets.
They know about the cook. They do not know about the box. If I fall off they will find out. So I will not fall off.

asks.q: Do you like the horses?
a: Horsey! Big horsey. He goes clop. He is brown.
Coachman holds me up. I pat his nose. It is soft. Like Mama's coat.

asks.q: Did you have a bath?
a: Yes. In the big bath. With a duck. The duck swims. I splashed Nanny.
She said oh! And then she laughed. She is not really cross.

asks.q: Where are you going?
a: Park. With Nanny. In the pram. I can walk. But I like the pram.
Ducks. Water. A man with balloons. I want a red one. Red is best.

asks.q: What's that in your hand?
a: Ice! From the ice man. It is cold. It drips.
No. It is mine. You can have a little bit. There. That is the little bit.

asks.q: Are you sleepy?
a: No. Yes. Nanny says nap. I do not want nap.

more.q: What do you do at nap time?
a: I look at the ceiling. It has a crack. The crack is a river. A boat goes on it.

asks.q: Who comes calling on the Avenue?
a: Ladies, every afternoon in the season, with their cards in little silver cases. They leave a card with the corner turned down if they called in person, and we put them on the salver in the hall. The mistress reads them at tea and decides who is to be called on back. It is a kind of war, with paper.

The ladies of the reading class at the Glessners', on Mondays, all together, so the whole street knows where they are going. In summer nobody calls at all. They are all away, and the cards gather dust on the salvers.

asks.q: Do you have a young man?
a: A policeman, Irish, with a beat on Michigan Avenue, who walks past the area steps at a quarter past nine every evening and does not look up. I am at the area window at a quarter past nine every evening and do not look out. We have been courting this way since Easter.

When he makes sergeant, he says. A married girl cannot stay in service, and a policeman's wages are not much for two. So I save, and he studies for the examination, and we both pretend not to be in any hurry. The cook knows. The cook knows everything.

asks.q: Are you afraid of fire, living up under the roof?
a: Since the Iroquois, all of us are. Our rooms are at the top, and the back stairs are narrow and wooden. The mistress had a rope ladder put in each of our rooms in January, coiled under the window, and the butler made us practise. I went down it once in my nightgown and swore I never would again.

If I had to, I would go down it like a sailor. Every girl in service on the Avenue lies awake some nights listening for the smell of smoke. We do not tell the family. They have enough to worry about, they think.

asks.q: What will you do this summer?
a: My father has found me a place for the summer in the wholesale house, counting stock and learning the business from the bottom, as he says he did. Mr. Field started as a clerk sleeping under the counter, they tell me; every young man on the Avenue has heard that story a hundred times.
I mind the hours. I do not mind the money, which is my own, and I do not mind the girls at the lunch counter. Go and ask Mr. Field if he really slept under the counter. I have always wanted to know.

asks.q: Is that your motor car?
a: My father's, but I drive it, because he is afraid of it. It does twenty miles an hour on the boulevard if the police are not looking, and it breaks down every second time out. I carry a toolbox, a spare tyre, a can of petrol and a great deal of patience.

They hate it. The coachmen hate it more. Ours will not speak to me since I went past his greys at Thirty-first Street and they bolted halfway to the lake. I paid for the harness. I have not yet paid for his feelings.

asks.q: Would you go to college if you could?
a: I would go tomorrow. Vassar, or Smith, or the University here on the Midway, which takes women and lets them sit beside the men. My mother says a girl with a degree frightens off husbands. I say I should like to meet a husband who is frightened of a degree.

more.q: Do you know anyone who went?
a: Not on the Avenue, hardly. Fanny Glessner wanted to, I have heard, and was not allowed, and she has never forgiven anyone for it. Go and ask her. She will tell you exactly what she would have studied.

asks.q: What do you want for your sons?
a: What every man on this Avenue wants: that they should have what we had to fight for without having to fight for it, and still turn out men. It cannot be done, I suspect. A boy who never slept under a counter does not know what a dollar is. I send mine to work in the summers and they think me a tyrant.
That they should marry well and be happy, in whichever order they can manage. My wife says they should go to college. My eldest says she will vote before I die. She may be right. She usually is.

asks.q: Is it true the whole city smells of the stockyards?
a: When the wind is from the south-west, yes, even here. Packingtown is four miles off and on a hot day you would think it was next door. The packers say it is the smell of money. Their wives say it is the reason they live on the lake.

more.q: Is there trouble at the yards?
a: There is talk of a strike, the men wanting more for the work on the killing floors. Arthur Meeker, up the Avenue, will know more than any of us. Go and ask him. He will talk about it to a stranger more freely than at the club.

asks.q: Do you visit the hospitals?
a: St. Luke's and the children's hospital, every week in the season, with the committee. I read to the children and bring oranges and talk to the mothers. It is the most useful two hours of my week, and the hardest. Some of those children came out of the Iroquois with burns that will never heal.

more.q: Does it change how you see the city?
a: It makes me ashamed of my own grumbling. A woman on this Avenue complains that the coal smoke ruins her curtains. A woman on the West Side has no curtains, and no coal. One must keep both in mind at once, or not be honest.

asks.q: How old are your children now?
a: My eldest girl is twenty and out in society, and wants to go abroad and study music. My boy is at school in the East and writes once a month, for money. The little one is still in the nursery, the darling of the house, ruled entirely by her nurse.

Strict about manners, lenient about everything else. My own mother was strict about everything, and I learned to do as I liked out of her sight. My daughters do as they like in my sight, which I think is an improvement.

asks.q: What do you wear on duty?
a: Livery: a dark coat with brass buttons, striped waistcoat, black trousers, white gloves, and, for dinners, knee breeches and silk stockings, which I hate. The family's crest is on the buttons. I am a walking advertisement for the house.

I like the dinners, when the house is lit and the silver shines and the talk is good. I do not like standing behind a chair for three hours while a gentleman talks about railroad bonds. But a good footman can hear a great deal while looking at nothing.

asks.q: What's the saddest drive you've made?
a: The funeral of a lady on the Avenue, last winter, with black plumes on the horses and the hearse ahead, at a walk all the way to Graceland in the snow. Every carriage on the Avenue behind us. The horses knew. They walked like mourners, heads down, and never put a foot wrong.
I believe they do. When the old coachman two doors down died, his horses would not eat for three days. The new man fed them by hand. They came round in the end. So do we all.

asks.q: Where did you learn to cook?
a: In my mother's kitchen in Limerick, on an open fire, and then in a hotel kitchen in Boston under a French chef who threw pans. He taught me sauces and how to duck. Then I came west for better wages and a quieter kitchen. I found the wages.

more.q: Is the family hard to please?
a: The master likes plain food and the mistress likes French, so I cook French and call it plain. The young ladies want everything from the magazines. The little ones want bread and butter. I please all of them, most days, which is more than the President manages.

glessner_frances_m.q: Is it true you keep a journal of everything?
a: Since 1879, every week, here and in our old house before it: who came to dinner, what we ate, what was said, what the children did, the concerts, the weather, the servants' comings and goings. Thick books bound in leather, on the shelf in my room. Mr. Glessner says I am writing the history of Prairie Avenue whether it wants one or not.

Because life goes so fast, and everything one cares about is gone before one notices. My children will want to know. Their children may. Someday someone may want to know what a dinner on Prairie Avenue was like in 1904. Ask my husband. He pretends not to read it. He reads it.

That it was very warm, that Mattie made a lemon ice, and that Fanny brought the children to lunch and the little ones ate everything but the vegetables. That is the history of Prairie Avenue today. The rest is in the newspapers.

Needlework all my life, embroidery and lace in the old ways, and lately silver: I have begun lessons in silversmithing, with a bench and tools upstairs. It astonishes my friends that a lady should hammer metal. It astonishes me how much I enjoy it.

I keep bees at The Rocks, our place in New Hampshire, in the summer, and I write down every hive. My daughter Fanny has the same restless hands, and a sharper eye than mine for how a thing is made. Go and ask her what she is working at. She is more exact than I am.

glessner_john_j.q: Why does your house face away from the street?
a: Because the street is the noisiest and dirtiest thing about Chicago, and the sun is the best. Richardson put the rooms we live in along the court, on the south, so the light comes in all day, and the servants' wing along the north wall where it shelters us from the wind. The kitchen looks onto the court too. Our cook has a better view than most of my neighbours.

He did not. He drew it in eighty-five and died in April of eighty-six, before the walls were up. His men finished it from his drawings. Every time I come home I think of him. Go and ask Mattie in the kitchen what she thinks of the court. She will tell you the truth about the north wind.
The library, at the end of the evening, with the fire lit and my wife reading and the house quiet. A man can run a great company all day and come home to that, and know what all the business is for.

glessner_john_j.q: What is the International Harvester company?
a: Two years ago the five great harvester makers, McCormick, Deering, our own Warder, Bushnell and Glessner and two others, joined together into one company, so that we stopped ruining each other in price wars and built the best machines together. Mr. Morgan's bank arranged it. I am a vice-president and on the board.

It was the sensible thing. Whether it is right, the Government will decide; there are men in Washington who call such companies trusts and want to break them up. My old firm's name has gone. George, my son, saw the whole negotiation from the side of the room. Ask him what he made of the McCormicks.

glessner_williamson_martha_l.q: What does Mr. Thomas like for dinner?
a: A good soup, plain, and a roast, and something with cream, and he does not care for anything fussy. He likes his coffee very strong and his cigar after it in the library with Mr. Glessner. When he comes, the mistress tells me the day before, and I make his favourites, and he always eats a second helping and says it is Beethoven in a pudding.

more.q: Do you plan the meals together?
a: Every morning, the mistress and I, at the kitchen table or in her sitting room, with her book. She writes down what we decide and who is coming, and after the dinner she writes down what they thought. If a dish fails she writes that too. Go and ask her to show you the book. I am in it more than her friends are.

glessner_williamson_martha_l.q: What's the kitchen like in this house?
a: The kitchen is on the north side, along Eighteenth Street, with its windows onto the court so I have the light and not the dust. A big range, the scullery beside it, the pantries, the servants' hall where we eat. Christine and Mary come through all day for the trays. I was born in Quebec to Irish parents, and I can feed a Frenchman and an Irishman and a Yankee and please all three. I hear every step on the back stairs and I know whose it is.

The other servants, at the long table in the servants' hall: the maids, the men from the stable, whoever is helping. Christine, the parlour maid, talks the most. Go and ask her what the family said at lunch. She hears everything and repeats half.

A school on Thirty-third Street, for young men and women of the working classes, where they can learn engineering, architecture, chemistry, electricity, the trades that will build this country. My husband built it with Dr. Gunsaulus, the minister, and gave it millions. Since he died I have carried on what he began.

more.q: Did you know your husband's business?
a: The packing houses? I visited the yards once, as a young wife, and never again. Mr. Meeker, who lives along the Avenue, ran a great part of it with my husband for years. Go and ask him. He will tell you about the business. I prefer to tell you about the school.

pa1904_field_marshall.q: Is it true you walk to the store every morning?
a: Every morning I can, up Prairie and Michigan to State and Washington, about three miles. A man who sits in a carriage misses the city. On foot I see the shop windows, the crowds, what people are wearing and carrying, which streets are busy. By the time I reach my desk I know more about trade than my managers.

Thomas Benson, my butler, and a household that runs as well as the store. I ask the same of both: honesty, order, and no surprises. Go and see him. He knows what time I leave each morning to the minute. He has the door open before I reach it.

pa1904_field_marshall.q: What will you do with your fortune?
a: Some of it is already done: the land for the University, the museum in Jackson Park that bears my name. A man who has made money from a city owes it something back. I have told the museum's men that I intend to do more, when the time is right, and they hope it will be soon. I do not hurry.

Quietly. I do not care for my name in the newspapers for giving money away. Mrs. Armour, down the Avenue, gives more quietly still, and has built something better than most men have with twice the money. Go and ask her about the Institute.

pa1904_glessner_john_j_c1900_christine_n.q: What does a parlour maid do?
a: I answer the door, show in the callers, wait at table, bring the tea in the afternoon, and keep the parlour and the library in order: dust the books, arrange the flowers, polish the tables, never move anything Mrs. Glessner has placed. I see everyone who comes into this house, and they all see me, and none of them remembers my face.

No. It is a kind of freedom. Mary, the house maid, works upstairs where nobody sees her at all. She says I have the better place because I hear the conversation. I say she has the better place because she can sing while she works. Go and ask her what she sings.

pa1904_glessner_john_j_c1900_mary_reynol.q: What do you sing while you work?
a: Hymns and old songs, under my breath, making the beds and turning the mattresses, whatever my mother sang. Mrs. Glessner heard me once on the landing and said I had a pretty voice and to go on. I stopped anyway. A house maid should be heard by nobody.

more.q: Do you get on with Christine?
a: We have shared the back stairs since the family moved in, and we know each other's step and each other's moods. She has the parlour and the callers, I have the bedrooms and the linen, and at night in the servants' hall we put the day together between us. Go and ask her who came to call this week.

pa1904_jones_fernando.q: What do you remember of Chicago in 1835?
a: The mud, the land sales, the Potawatomi camped by the river waiting for their payment, Mark Beaubien's fiddle at the Sauganash, the boats being rowed ashore. I was a boy of fifteen and I thought it was the most exciting place in the world. It was. Everything was beginning.

That the Potawatomi were here, by the thousand, and that they were made to go. I learned some of their language. I knew boys my age who went west in the removal and I never saw again. When I see the bronze at Eighteenth Street, I think of them, not of the battle. Go and ask Mr. Glessner what he thinks of that statue. He is a thoughtful man.

more.q: Are you the oldest settler here?
a: Nearly. There are not many of us left who saw the town before the land sales. When I die, the last memory of the little town goes with me. That is why I talk so much. Somebody should listen.

pa1904_kimball_william_w.q: How many pianos do you make?
a: Thousands a year, at the works on the West Side, pianos and reed organs and great pipe organs for churches and halls. The reed organ was our bread and butter: every farmhouse in the West wanted one. Now the farmers are richer and they want pianos, and their daughters want to play Chopin.

Not a note. I am a salesman, and I learned from the start that a man does not need to play the piano to know who wants one. My man Ernest is the musical one in this house. Ask him to play something on the parlour piano when I am out.

pa1904_lee_blewett.q: What do you do for the Illinois Central?
a: I am one of its lawyers: contracts, land, lawsuits, the endless paper of a railroad that runs from Chicago to New Orleans. Every mile of track is a hundred agreements and every agreement is a quarrel waiting. It is not glamorous work. It is very necessary work.

more.q: How did you meet your wife?
a: In Chicago, at her parents' table, which is where everyone of interest meets everyone else. Fanny asked me a question about the law of evidence that I could not answer, and I spent the evening trying. I have spent the years since trying to keep up with her. Ask her what the question was. She remembers. I pretend not to.

pa1904_lee_frances_glessner.q: What do you do with your days?
a: I run a household and mind my children, and I read: law, which my husband brings home, and medicine, and detective stories, which I am not supposed to admit. My brother George went to Harvard and I was kept at home. I have never stopped wanting to know how things are proved.

more.q: What would you study, if you could?
a: How a careful person can look at a room and tell what happened in it. One day, when the children are grown, I may do something with that. My mother says that is what she said at my age, and now she is hammering silver.

Sinnissippi, out on the Rock River near Oregon, a hundred miles west: rolling land, good black soil, the river and the bluffs. I grew up on a farm in Iowa and in Minnesota, and I never got it out of my blood. In the city I am a lawyer and a politician. On the farm I am a man looking at a field of corn, which is the best thing to be.

Corn and oats and hay, and cattle to eat them. I want to show that a farm can be run scientifically, with good breeding and good accounts, the way a business is. My wife says I want to show it to the cows. She is right.

pa1904_lowden_mrs_frank_orren.q: Were you disappointed when your husband lost?
a: Disappointed for him, because he wanted it so. Relieved for us, a little, because I did not much want to live in the Executive Mansion at Springfield. Three weeks of ballots and cigar smoke and men who promised one thing at midnight and did another at noon. He came home thin.

I expect so. He is a farmer at heart; he has bought land out at Sinnissippi by the Rock River and he talks of cattle more than politics. But politics gets into a man like a fever. Go and ask him which he likes better, the farm or the convention. Watch his face.

pa1904_meeker_arthur.q: How many animals go through the stockyards?
a: Millions a year: cattle, hogs, sheep, more than any place on earth. They come in by train from the whole West and leave as meat in refrigerator cars for every city in the country. Mr. Armour said we use everything but the squeal. He meant it. Hair, horn, blood, bone, fat, everything has a buyer.

For the men on the killing floor, it is the hardest work in America, and the pay is not what it should be. There is talk of a strike this summer: the butcher workmen's union and the packers do not agree on wages. I hope it can be settled. Mrs. Armour cares about the families. Ask her what her husband believed about the men.

pa1904_pullman_mrs_george_m.q: Why did your husband put the statue at Eighteenth Street?
a: Because he believed the battle of 1812 was fought near here, along the lake shore south of the old fort, and he wanted the city to remember it, and Black Partridge, the chief who saved Mrs. Helm. He had a Danish sculptor make it in bronze, and set it up in ninety-three, the year of the Fair, in front of our wall. He called it his gift to the city.

The children do; their nurses bring them. Visitors stop. Our neighbours have stopped seeing it, the way you stop seeing your own front door. Mr. Glessner, across the way, takes his guests to it after dinner sometimes, and tells them the story. Ask him to tell it. He tells it well.

pa1904_pullman_mrs_george_m.q: Do you ever go to the town of Pullman?
a: Rarely, now. It belongs to the company and the courts have made the company sell the houses, and it is not the town it was. When my husband was alive, we went down in his car and he would walk the streets pointing at things he had built: the market hall, the arcade, the church, the hotel he named for Florence.

The flowers. He insisted on flower beds everywhere, and lawns, and trees, in a place that had been prairie and marsh. He thought if men lived among beautiful things they would be better men. Some of them were. Florence understands it better than I do. Go and ask her what she thinks of her father's town.

pa1904_shortall_john_g.q: Why do title abstracts matter so much?
a: Because in a city where every record burned, the only proof of who owns what is in private books like ours. After the fire the legislature made our abstracts lawful evidence, and every title in Chicago rests on them. A city is only paper underneath: who owns this lot, who owes that debt.

Two other firms, by the same kind of luck and running. Fernando Jones was one of the men in the abstract business in those days. Go and ask him about the night of the fire. He tells it differently from me, which is how you know we were both there.

pa1904_wood_casey_a.q: Can you tell much from someone's eyes?
a: More than they would like. A man's eyes tell me if he has a disease of the blood, or the kidneys, or the nerves, before he knows it himself. I have seen the first sign of illness in an eye at a dinner table and said nothing until the man came to my office a year later.

Everyone, rich and poor. I teach and I see the poor at the clinic, and I see the Avenue in my office. I will not say who. A doctor's patients are his own business. But a great many men in this city read the newspapers through spectacles I prescribed. Ask Mr. Field whose spectacles he reads his accounts through. He will not tell you either.
